sections.title: Amazon Athena
sections.summary: Serverless SQL queries directly on data in Amazon S3; you pay for the data each query scans.

items.name: What Athena does
items.summary: Run standard SQL on files in S3 without loading them into a database or managing servers.
items.details: Athena is serverless. You point it at data in S3 (CSV, JSON, Parquet, logs), define a table, often with the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and query it with SQL. You pay for the amount of data each query scans.
items.example: An analyst queries a year of CloudTrail logs stored in S3 to find who deleted a bucket.
items.tip: Ad hoc SQL on data already in S3, no infrastructure → Athena. A data warehouse for repeated, complex analytics → Redshift.

items.name: Keeping Athena queries cheap
items.summary: Compress, partition, and use columnar formats such as Parquet so each query scans less data.
items.details: Because pricing is per data scanned, compressed columnar formats and partitions (for example by date) let each query read only the data it needs.
items.example: Partitioning logs by day lets a query about yesterday scan one day of data instead of a whole year.
items.tip: Athena cost depends on data scanned, not on servers or query time.

sections.title: Amazon EMR
sections.summary: Managed big data platform for Apache Spark, Hadoop, Hive, and similar open-source frameworks.

items.name: Big data processing
items.summary: Run frameworks such as Spark and Hadoop on managed clusters, on EKS, or serverless.
items.details: EMR provisions and manages the clusters that run big data frameworks to process very large datasets, for example ETL, log processing, and preparing data for ML.
items.example: A media company processes petabytes of clickstream data every night with Spark on EMR.
items.tip: Spark or Hadoop named in the question → EMR. SQL on S3 without clusters → Athena.

sections.title: AWS Glue
sections.summary: Serverless data integration: ETL jobs, crawlers, and the Glue Data Catalog.

items.name: Serverless ETL
items.summary: Extract, transform, and load data between sources without managing servers.
items.details: Glue runs serverless ETL jobs that clean and reshape data, for example converting CSV to Parquet or joining datasets, and loads the results into targets such as S3 or Redshift.
items.example: A retailer converts its daily CSV sales exports into Parquet for faster, cheaper Athena queries.
items.tip: ETL with no servers to manage → AWS Glue.

items.name: Crawlers and the Data Catalog
items.summary: Crawlers detect schemas and register tables in a central metadata catalog.
items.details: A Glue crawler scans a data store, detects the format and schema, and records the table in the Glue Data Catalog. Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum use the catalog to find and query the data.
items.example: A crawler notices new columns in log files and updates the table definition automatically.
items.tip: Athena usually relies on the Glue Data Catalog for its table definitions.

sections.title: Amazon Kinesis
sections.summary: Collect and process streaming data in real time, such as clickstreams, logs, and IoT telemetry.

items.name: Kinesis Data Streams
items.summary: Real-time data streams that applications read and process within milliseconds.
items.details: Producers write records to a stream, and consumer applications read and process them in real time. Records are kept for 24 hours by default, and retention can be extended.
items.example: A game company processes player events in real time to update a live leaderboard.
items.tip: Real-time streaming ingestion → Kinesis. A message queue between application components → SQS.

items.name: Amazon Data Firehose
items.summary: Loads streaming data into destinations such as S3, Redshift, and OpenSearch with no code.
items.details: Firehose (formerly Kinesis Data Firehose) captures streaming data, can batch, compress, and transform it, and delivers it to storage and analytics destinations. It is fully managed and scales automatically.
items.example: Web server logs are delivered to S3 every minute for later analysis with Athena.
items.tip: Load streaming data into S3 or Redshift with the least effort → Data Firehose.

sections.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service
sections.summary: Managed search and log analytics with OpenSearch and OpenSearch Dashboards.

items.name: Search and log analytics
items.summary: Full-text search, log analytics, and dashboards on managed clusters or serverless collections.
items.details: OpenSearch Service runs OpenSearch for searching text and analyzing logs and metrics in near real time, with OpenSearch Dashboards for visualization. A serverless option removes cluster management.
items.example: An online store adds fast, typo-tolerant search across its product catalog.
items.tip: Full-text search or log analytics dashboards → OpenSearch Service.

sections.title: Amazon Quick Sight
sections.summary: Business intelligence dashboards and visualizations, part of Amazon Quick.

items.name: Dashboards and BI
items.summary: Build interactive dashboards and reports from many data sources and share them with users.
items.details: Quick Sight (formerly QuickSight) is the business intelligence capability of Amazon Quick. It connects to sources such as Athena, Redshift, RDS, and S3 and lets users explore data with visuals and natural-language questions.
items.example: Executives check a weekly sales dashboard built on data in Redshift.
items.tip: Visualize data in dashboards → Quick Sight. Query data with SQL → Athena or Redshift.

sections.title: Amazon Redshift
sections.summary: Fully managed, petabyte-scale cloud data warehouse for SQL analytics.

items.name: Data warehouse (OLAP)
items.summary: Columnar data warehouse for fast analytical queries on large amounts of structured data.
items.details: Redshift stores data in columns and runs complex queries in parallel across nodes. It suits reporting and analytics on historical data, not an application’s day-to-day transactions. Redshift Serverless removes cluster management.
items.example: A retailer analyzes five years of sales across regions and product lines.
items.tip: Analytics on large historical datasets (OLAP) → Redshift. Transactions for an application (OLTP) → RDS or Aurora.

sections.title: Amazon EventBridge
sections.summary: Serverless event bus that routes events from AWS services, SaaS apps, and your apps to targets.

items.name: Event routing
items.summary: Rules match events and send them to targets such as Lambda, SQS, or Step Functions.
items.details: EventBridge receives events, such as an EC2 instance changing state or a new ticket in a SaaS app, and uses rules to route matching events to targets. It enables loosely coupled, event-driven applications.
items.example: When an EC2 instance stops, a rule triggers a Lambda function that notifies the team.
items.tip: React to events from AWS services or SaaS applications → EventBridge.

items.name: EventBridge Scheduler
items.summary: Run tasks on a schedule, such as every hour or with a cron expression.
items.details: EventBridge Scheduler invokes targets at a specific time or on a recurring schedule, so you don’t need a server that runs cron jobs.
items.example: A Lambda function that deletes temporary files runs every night at 2 AM.
items.tip: Serverless scheduled tasks (cron) → EventBridge Scheduler.

sections.title: Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS)
sections.summary: Pub/sub messaging that pushes each message to many subscribers: email, SMS, Lambda, SQS, HTTP.

items.name: Publish/subscribe and fan-out
items.summary: One message published to a topic is pushed to every subscriber at once.
items.details: Publishers send messages to an SNS topic, and SNS immediately pushes copies to all subscribers. Combined with SQS queues, this fan-out pattern lets several systems process the same event independently.
items.example: An order event goes to separate SQS queues for billing, shipping, and analytics.
items.tip: One-to-many push → SNS. A queue that consumers pull from → SQS.

items.name: Alerts and notifications
items.summary: Send email or SMS alerts, for example from CloudWatch alarms or AWS Budgets.
items.details: SNS is the usual way to deliver notifications to people. CloudWatch alarms and other services publish to a topic, and subscribers receive the message by email, SMS, or mobile push.
items.example: A CloudWatch alarm for high CPU emails the operations team through an SNS topic.
items.tip: Send an alert or notification → SNS.

sections.title: Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS)
sections.summary: Fully managed message queues that decouple components so they scale and fail independently.

items.name: Decoupling with queues
items.summary: Producers add messages to a queue; consumers pull and process them at their own pace.
items.details: SQS stores messages until a consumer processes and deletes them, so a traffic spike or a slow consumer doesn’t overwhelm the rest of the system. Standard queues offer very high throughput; FIFO queues keep messages in order and process each one exactly once.
items.example: A web tier puts image-resize jobs in a queue, and worker instances process them as capacity allows.
items.tip: Decouple components or buffer requests → SQS. Strict ordering → an SQS FIFO queue.

sections.title: AWS Step Functions
sections.summary: Visual workflows that coordinate Lambda functions and AWS services, with retries and error handling.

items.name: Workflow orchestration
items.summary: Define multi-step workflows as state machines with branches, retries, and parallel steps.
items.details: Step Functions coordinates the steps of a process, such as validate, charge, and ship. It tracks the state of each run and handles errors and retries, so that logic doesn’t have to live in custom code.
items.example: An order process calls several Lambda functions in sequence and waits for a manager’s approval.
items.tip: Coordinate several steps or services in a defined order → Step Functions.

sections.title: Amazon Connect
sections.summary: Cloud contact center for voice and chat customer service, with pay-as-you-go pricing.

items.name: Cloud contact center
items.summary: Set up a customer service contact center in minutes, with no phone hardware.
items.details: Connect provides phone and chat channels, call routing, an agent workspace, and analytics. It integrates with AI services such as Amazon Lex for self-service bots.
items.example: A retailer opens a seasonal support line and pays only for the minutes used.
items.tip: Contact center or call center → Amazon Connect.

sections.title: Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES)
sections.summary: Send transactional and marketing email at scale from your applications.

items.name: Transactional and bulk email
items.summary: Send emails such as order confirmations, password resets, and newsletters from applications.
items.details: SES is an email platform for sending large volumes of formatted email to customers, with tools to improve deliverability. It can also receive email.
items.example: An online shop sends an HTML order confirmation to every customer.
items.tip: Marketing or transactional email to customers → SES. Simple alert notifications → SNS.

sections.title: AWS Budgets
sections.summary: Set cost and usage budgets and get alerts when spend exceeds, or is forecast to exceed, them.

items.name: Budget alerts
items.summary: Alerts by email or SNS when actual or forecasted spend crosses a threshold you set.
items.details: You set a budget amount and alert thresholds, and AWS Budgets notifies you. Budget actions can also apply an IAM policy or SCP, or stop instances, when a threshold is reached.
items.example: A team gets an email when forecasted monthly spend will exceed $500.
items.tip: Alert before you overspend → AWS Budgets. Analyze past spend → Cost Explorer.

items.name: Zero-spend budget
items.summary: A template budget that alerts you as soon as any spend appears.
items.details: A zero-spend budget is a simple guardrail for learners and free-tier users: it emails you when your account incurs its first charge.
items.example: A student is alerted after forgetting a resource that started to cost money.
items.tip: Create a budget before experimenting in a new account.

sections.title: AWS Cost and Usage Reports
sections.summary: The most detailed billing data, delivered to S3 for analysis with Athena or BI tools.

items.name: Detailed billing data
items.summary: Line-item cost and usage data, including resource IDs and tags, delivered to an S3 bucket.
items.details: Cost and Usage Reports (CUR, now delivered through Data Exports) list every line item of usage with resource IDs and cost allocation tags. Teams analyze them with Athena, Redshift, or Quick Sight.
items.example: A finance team builds a chargeback report for each department from tagged usage.
items.tip: Most granular billing data for your own analysis → Cost and Usage Reports.

sections.title: AWS Cost Explorer
sections.summary: Visualize, filter, and forecast your AWS costs and usage over time.

items.name: Analyze and forecast costs
items.summary: Graphs of spend by service, account, Region, or tag, with history and a forecast.
items.details: Cost Explorer shows where money goes, lets you filter and group by dimensions such as service and cost allocation tag, and forecasts future spend. It also recommends Savings Plans and Reserved Instance purchases.
items.example: A manager sees that EC2 costs doubled last month in one Region.
items.tip: Understand past and current spending trends → Cost Explorer.

sections.title: AWS Marketplace
sections.summary: Catalog to find, buy, and deploy third-party software, data, and services that run on AWS.

items.name: Third-party software catalog
items.summary: Buy software from independent vendors, with charges on your AWS bill.
items.details: Marketplace lists products such as security tools, databases, and SaaS applications from independent software vendors (ISVs). Many deploy directly into your account, and charges appear on your AWS bill.
items.example: A security team subscribes to a third-party firewall appliance and launches it in its VPC.
items.tip: Third-party security products or software for AWS → AWS Marketplace.

items.name: Governance and entitlements
items.summary: Private offers, private marketplaces, and license tracking help control spending and approved software.
items.details: Customers can negotiate private offers with sellers, curate an approved catalog with a private marketplace, and track entitlements. The exam guide calls out cost management, governance, and entitlement as key Marketplace capabilities.
items.example: IT lets employees buy only approved products through a private marketplace.

sections.title: Amazon EC2
sections.summary: Resizable virtual servers (instances) in the cloud, with full control of the operating system.

items.name: Virtual servers
items.summary: Launch instances from an AMI, choose the instance type, storage, and network, and pay while they run.
items.details: EC2 gives you virtual machines with full control over the operating system and software. You choose an Amazon Machine Image (AMI), an instance type, storage, and security groups. You are responsible for patching the guest OS.
items.example: A company lifts and shifts a legacy Windows application onto EC2.
items.tip: Full control of the OS or custom software → EC2.

items.name: Instance families
items.summary: General purpose, compute optimized, memory optimized, storage optimized, and accelerated computing.
items.details: Each family suits a type of workload: general purpose (balanced, such as web servers), compute optimized (high CPU, such as batch processing and gaming), memory optimized (large in-memory datasets), storage optimized (high local disk I/O), and accelerated computing (GPUs for ML and graphics).
items.example: An in-memory analytics engine runs on a memory-optimized instance.
items.tip: Match the bottleneck: CPU → compute optimized; RAM → memory optimized; local disk I/O → storage optimized.

items.name: Stop vs terminate
items.summary: Stopping keeps EBS volumes (storage is still billed); terminating deletes the instance.
items.details: A stopped instance has no compute charges, but its EBS volumes still cost money. Terminating deletes the instance and, by default, its root volume. Instance store data is lost when an instance stops or terminates.
items.example: A developer stops a test instance overnight to save compute costs.
items.tip: Stopped isn’t free: EBS volumes and public IPv4 addresses can still be charged.

sections.title: Elastic Load Balancing
sections.summary: Distributes incoming traffic across healthy targets in multiple Availability Zones.

items.name: Load balancers
items.summary: Spread traffic across instances, containers, or IP addresses and route around unhealthy targets.
items.details: A load balancer runs health checks and sends traffic only to healthy targets across several AZs, which improves availability and fault tolerance. Application Load Balancers route HTTP/HTTPS by path or host; Network Load Balancers handle very high-performance TCP/UDP traffic.
items.example: An Application Load Balancer sends /api requests to one group of instances and /images to another.
items.tip: Distribute traffic and improve availability → Elastic Load Balancing. Change the number of instances → Auto Scaling.

sections.title: AWS Batch
sections.summary: Run batch computing jobs at any scale; AWS provisions the compute capacity.

items.name: Managed batch jobs
items.summary: Submit jobs to queues; Batch provisions EC2, Spot, or Fargate capacity to run them.
items.details: Batch plans, schedules, and runs large numbers of batch jobs and chooses the amount and type of compute. It can use Spot Instances to reduce cost.
items.example: A research lab runs 10,000 genome analysis jobs over a weekend.
items.tip: Large numbers of batch jobs without managing a cluster → AWS Batch.

sections.title: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
sections.summary: Upload your code; Beanstalk handles provisioning, load balancing, scaling, and monitoring.

items.name: Platform as a service
items.summary: Deploy web apps in Java, .NET, Node.js, Python, and more without managing infrastructure details.
items.details: You upload code, and Beanstalk creates and manages the EC2 instances, load balancer, Auto Scaling, and health monitoring. You keep access to the underlying resources and pay only for them.
items.example: A developer deploys a Python web app by uploading a zip file.
items.tip: Deploy an app quickly without managing infrastructure (PaaS) → Elastic Beanstalk. Define infrastructure as code → CloudFormation.

sections.title: Amazon Lightsail
sections.summary: Simple virtual private servers, databases, and networking for a low, predictable monthly price.

items.name: Simple VPS bundles
items.summary: Bundles of compute, storage, and data transfer for simple websites and small applications.
items.details: Lightsail is designed for people with little cloud experience who want a simple website, blog, or small app with predictable pricing, using ready-made blueprints such as WordPress.
items.example: A small business launches a WordPress site for a fixed monthly price.
items.tip: Simple website, predictable monthly price, minimal cloud knowledge → Lightsail.

sections.title: AWS Outposts
sections.summary: AWS-managed racks and servers that run AWS services in your own data center.

items.name: AWS on premises
items.summary: Run AWS infrastructure and services on premises for low latency or local data processing.
items.details: Outposts brings AWS hardware, APIs, and tools into your data center, managed by AWS. It suits workloads that need low latency to on-premises systems or must keep data on site.
items.example: A factory runs EC2 instances next to its production line for millisecond latency.
items.tip: AWS services in your own data center (hybrid) → Outposts. AWS infrastructure closer to a metro area → Local Zones.

sections.title: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR)
sections.summary: Managed registry to store, share, and deploy container images.

items.name: Container image registry
items.summary: Store container images privately or publicly, with access control and vulnerability scanning.
items.details: ECR stores the container images that ECS, EKS, and Fargate pull when they deploy. It uses IAM for access and can scan images for vulnerabilities with Amazon Inspector.
items.example: A build pipeline pushes a new image to ECR after every successful build.
items.tip: Store container images → ECR. Run containers → ECS or EKS.

sections.title: Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS)
sections.summary: AWS-native container orchestration to run and scale containers on EC2 or Fargate.

items.name: Container orchestration
items.summary: Define tasks and services; ECS places, runs, and scales your containers.
items.details: ECS is AWS’s own container orchestrator. It schedules containers on EC2 instances that you manage or on serverless Fargate, and integrates with load balancers and IAM.
items.example: A team runs its microservices as ECS services behind an Application Load Balancer.
items.tip: Run containers with AWS-native tooling → ECS. Need Kubernetes → EKS.

sections.title: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS)
sections.summary: Managed Kubernetes control plane for running Kubernetes workloads on AWS.

items.name: Managed Kubernetes
items.summary: AWS runs the Kubernetes control plane; workloads run on EC2 nodes or on Fargate.
items.details: EKS suits teams that already use Kubernetes or want portability between environments. AWS manages the availability of the control plane, and standard Kubernetes tools work unchanged.
items.example: A company moves its existing Kubernetes applications from on premises to AWS without rewriting them.
items.tip: Kubernetes named in the question → EKS.

sections.title: AWS Support
sections.summary: Support plans from Basic (free) to Unified Operations; account and billing help is included for everyone.

items.name: Basic Support
items.summary: Free: account and billing help, documentation, re:Post, Health Dashboard, and core Trusted Advisor checks.
items.details: Every account has Basic Support: 24/7 customer service for account and billing questions, documentation and whitepapers, AWS re:Post, the AWS Health Dashboard, and core Trusted Advisor checks. It doesn’t include technical support cases.
items.example: A hobbyist gets help with a billing question at no cost.
items.tip: Technical support cases need a paid support plan.

items.name: Business Support+
items.summary: From $29 a month: 24/7 access to AWS experts, AI-powered help, and all Trusted Advisor checks.
items.details: The entry paid plan for production workloads. It combines AI-assisted troubleshooting with 24/7 access to support engineers, a 30-minute response for critical issues, and the full set of Trusted Advisor checks. It doesn’t include a designated technical account manager (TAM).
items.example: A startup with production workloads wants 24/7 technical help without an enterprise contract.
items.tip: Lowest-cost plan with 24/7 technical support and all Trusted Advisor checks → Business Support+.

items.name: Enterprise Support
items.summary: From $5,000 a month: a designated technical account manager (TAM) and 15-minute critical response.
items.details: For business-critical workloads. A designated TAM gives architectural and operational guidance, leads Well-Architected reviews, and coordinates AWS experts. It includes Trusted Advisor Priority, AWS Countdown event support, and AWS Security Incident Response.
items.example: A bank wants a named TAM to review its architecture before a major product launch.
items.tip: Designated TAM → Enterprise Support (or Unified Operations).

items.name: Unified Operations
items.summary: From $50,000 a month: the fastest response (5 minutes), with incident management engineers.
items.details: The top tier for mission-critical workloads. It adds incident management engineers who respond within minutes, domain specialist engineers, proactive monitoring, and continuous architecture reviews.
items.example: A global payments company needs incident engineers engaged within 5 minutes of an outage.
items.tip: Fastest response and dedicated incident management → Unified Operations.

items.name: Legacy plans (ending 1 January 2027)
items.summary: Developer, Business, and Enterprise On-Ramp end in 2027, but AWS’s own practice questions still use them.
items.details: Developer Support (business-hours email, for testing), Business Support (24/7 phone and chat, full Trusted Advisor), and Enterprise On-Ramp (a pool of TAMs) end on 1 January 2027. Business Support+ and Enterprise Support replace them. The exam guide lists the new plans, but the official CLF practice question set (checked October 2026) still asks about the older ones.
items.example: The minimum older plan with 24/7 phone support → Business Support. The cheapest older plan with technical help for a test environment → Developer Support.
items.tip: Use whichever set of names the options use: older names → older rules; Business Support+, Enterprise, or Unified Operations → current rules.

sections.title: Amazon RDS
sections.summary: Managed relational databases: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, and Db2.

items.name: Managed relational database
items.summary: AWS handles provisioning, patching, backups, and recovery; you manage the schema and queries.
items.details: RDS runs common relational database engines without you managing the operating system or database software. It provides automated backups, point-in-time restore, and scaling options.
items.example: A company moves its MySQL database from an on-premises server to RDS to stop manual patching.
items.tip: Relational database with less management than running it yourself on EC2 → RDS.

items.name: Multi-AZ deployments
items.summary: A standby copy in another AZ with automatic failover, for high availability.
items.details: With Multi-AZ, RDS synchronously replicates data to a standby in a different Availability Zone and fails over automatically if the primary fails. It improves availability, not read performance.
items.example: A production order database keeps running when one AZ has an outage.
items.tip: High availability → Multi-AZ. More read capacity → read replicas.

items.name: Read replicas
items.summary: Asynchronous copies that serve read-only traffic to improve read performance.
items.details: Read replicas take read queries, such as reports, off the primary database. They can be in the same or another Region and can be promoted to a standalone database.
items.example: A reporting tool queries a read replica so it doesn’t slow down the production database.
items.tip: Read-heavy workload → read replicas.

items.name: Managed database vs a database on EC2
items.summary: Use RDS to offload operations; use EC2 when you need OS access or software RDS doesn’t support.
items.details: On EC2 you install, patch, back up, and make the database highly available yourself. RDS moves those tasks to AWS. You might still choose EC2 for a database engine or version that RDS doesn’t offer, or when the software needs OS-level access.
items.example: A vendor application needs OS-level access to its database server, so the team runs it on EC2.
items.tip: LEAST operational overhead for a relational database → RDS or Aurora, not EC2.

sections.title: Amazon Aurora
sections.summary: Cloud-native relational database, compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL, with higher performance and availability.

items.name: High-performance relational database
items.summary: Up to 5x MySQL and 3x PostgreSQL throughput; storage keeps six copies across three AZs.
items.details: Aurora is compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL but uses a distributed storage layer that keeps six copies of your data across three Availability Zones and grows automatically. Aurora Serverless adjusts capacity to demand.
items.example: An online game moves to Aurora MySQL for better performance without changing its queries.
items.tip: MySQL- or PostgreSQL-compatible with higher performance and availability → Aurora.

sections.title: Amazon DynamoDB
sections.summary: Serverless NoSQL key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond performance at any scale.

items.name: Serverless NoSQL
items.summary: Key-value and document data with no servers, automatic scaling, and consistently low latency.
items.details: DynamoDB is fully managed and serverless: you create tables, and AWS handles capacity, replication across AZs, and patching. It suits high-traffic apps with simple access patterns, such as user profiles, shopping carts, and gaming sessions.
items.example: A mobile game stores millions of player sessions with millisecond reads.
items.tip: NoSQL, key-value, serverless, massive scale → DynamoDB.

items.name: Global tables, on-demand capacity, and DAX
items.summary: Multi-Region replication, pay-per-request capacity, and an in-memory cache.
items.details: Global tables replicate data across Regions for low-latency global apps and disaster recovery. On-demand capacity charges per request, so you don’t plan capacity. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory cache for microsecond reads.
items.example: A global app uses global tables so users in Europe and Asia read from a nearby Region.
items.tip: Microsecond reads on DynamoDB → DAX.

sections.title: Amazon ElastiCache
sections.summary: Managed in-memory caching with Valkey, Redis OSS, or Memcached for microsecond latency.

items.name: In-memory cache
items.summary: Cache frequent database reads and session data in memory to cut latency and database load.
items.details: ElastiCache keeps data in memory, so reads take microseconds. Placing it in front of a database avoids repeating the same queries; it is also used for session stores and leaderboards.
items.example: A news site caches its most-read articles so the database isn’t queried on every page view.
items.tip: Speed up reads with an in-memory cache → ElastiCache.

sections.title: Amazon Neptune
sections.summary: Managed graph database for highly connected data.

items.name: Graph database
items.summary: Store and query relationships, such as social networks, fraud rings, and recommendations.
items.details: Neptune is built to traverse relationships between entities quickly, using graph query languages such as Gremlin, openCypher, and SPARQL.
items.example: A bank finds fraud rings by following accounts that share devices and addresses.
items.tip: Relationships between entities (social graph, fraud detection) → Neptune.

sections.title: Amazon DocumentDB
sections.summary: Managed document database with MongoDB compatibility.

items.name: MongoDB-compatible documents
items.summary: Store JSON-like documents; existing MongoDB applications and drivers work with few changes.
items.details: DocumentDB stores semi-structured JSON documents and supports MongoDB APIs, so teams can move MongoDB workloads without running the database themselves.
items.example: A content platform migrates its MongoDB product catalog to DocumentDB.
items.tip: MongoDB compatibility → DocumentDB.

sections.title: AWS CLI and AWS SDKs
sections.summary: Programmatic access to AWS from a terminal (CLI) or from application code (SDKs).

items.name: AWS CLI
items.summary: Command-line tool to manage AWS services and automate tasks with scripts.
items.details: The AWS Command Line Interface runs AWS API operations from a terminal, which makes repeated tasks scriptable. It authenticates with credentials such as temporary IAM Identity Center credentials or access keys.
items.example: An administrator writes a script that creates the same S3 buckets in every new account.
items.tip: Programmatic access from a terminal or scripts → AWS CLI.

items.name: AWS SDKs
items.summary: Libraries for languages such as Python, Java, and JavaScript that call AWS APIs from code.
items.details: SDKs wrap the AWS APIs for each programming language and handle authentication, retries, and request signing, so applications can use AWS services directly.
items.example: A Python app uploads user photos to S3 with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3).
items.tip: Call AWS services from application code → AWS SDKs.

items.name: Choosing an access method
items.summary: Console for one-off tasks; CLI and SDKs for automation; infrastructure as code for repeatable environments.
items.details: The Management Console is easiest for exploring and one-time actions. The CLI and SDKs automate tasks. Infrastructure as code, such as CloudFormation, defines whole environments in templates so they are repeatable and version-controlled.
items.example: A team builds identical dev, test, and production environments from one CloudFormation template.
items.tip: Repeatable environments → infrastructure as code. A one-time change → the console.

sections.title: AWS CodeBuild
sections.summary: Fully managed build service that compiles code, runs tests, and produces deployable artifacts.

items.name: Managed builds and tests
items.summary: Compile source code and run tests without managing build servers; pay for build minutes.
items.details: CodeBuild runs each build in a fresh container that scales automatically, so teams don’t maintain build servers. It is often one stage of a CodePipeline release.
items.example: Every commit triggers CodeBuild to run the unit tests and package the app.
items.tip: Compile code and run tests → CodeBuild.

sections.title: AWS CodePipeline
sections.summary: Continuous delivery service that automates the build, test, and deploy stages of a release.

items.name: CI/CD pipelines
items.summary: Model release stages (source, build, test, deploy) that run automatically on every change.
items.details: CodePipeline orchestrates the release process: it detects a code change, runs it through build and test stages (for example with CodeBuild), and deploys it, which makes releases fast and consistent.
items.example: A change merged to the main branch is built, tested, and deployed to production without manual steps.
items.tip: Automate the whole release process (CI/CD) → CodePipeline. Only the build step → CodeBuild.

sections.title: AWS X-Ray
sections.summary: Trace requests through distributed applications to find bottlenecks and errors.

items.name: Distributed tracing
items.summary: Follow a request across services to see where time is spent and where errors happen.
items.details: X-Ray collects traces from applications and AWS services and draws a service map, which helps developers troubleshoot latency and errors in microservices and serverless applications.
items.example: A developer finds that a slow checkout is caused by one downstream payment service.
items.tip: Trace requests across microservices → X-Ray. Metrics and alarms → CloudWatch.

sections.title: Amazon AppStream 2.0 (now Amazon WorkSpaces Applications)
sections.summary: Stream desktop applications to a web browser without installing them on users’ devices.

items.name: Application streaming
items.summary: Users run specific desktop applications from a browser while the app runs on AWS.
items.details: AppStream 2.0, renamed Amazon WorkSpaces Applications, streams individual applications rather than full desktops. Users connect from any device, and the application and data stay on AWS.
items.example: A university lets students use engineering software from their own laptops through a browser.
items.tip: Stream individual applications → AppStream 2.0. A full virtual desktop → WorkSpaces.

sections.title: Amazon WorkSpaces
sections.summary: Managed virtual desktops (desktop as a service) for Windows and Linux users.

items.name: Virtual desktops
items.summary: Give each user a persistent cloud desktop they can reach from almost any device.
items.details: WorkSpaces provides desktop as a service: AWS runs the virtual desktops, and users connect from laptops, thin clients, or browsers, so there is no desktop hardware to buy and manage.
items.example: A company gives contractors secure desktops without shipping them laptops.
items.tip: Virtual desktops (VDI, DaaS) → WorkSpaces.

sections.title: Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser
sections.summary: Streamed browser for internal websites and SaaS apps; closed to new customers from 29 October 2026.

items.name: Secure web access (closing to new customers)
items.summary: Users open internal web apps in a streamed browser; nothing lands on their device. New sign-ups end 29 Oct 2026.
items.details: WorkSpaces Secure Browser (formerly WorkSpaces Web) streams a browser session from AWS, so company web content never lands on the user’s device. AWS closes it to new customers on 29 October 2026, and existing customers keep using it. For new setups, AWS recommends WorkSpaces Applications (formerly AppStream 2.0) with a Chrome image, which gives the same pixel-streaming isolation.
items.example: Contractors use an internal HR portal from personal devices without being able to download files.
items.tip: The exam guide still lists it: secure access to web apps only, from unmanaged devices → WorkSpaces Secure Browser.

sections.title: AWS Amplify
sections.summary: Build, deploy, and host full-stack web and mobile apps quickly.

items.name: Full-stack web and mobile apps
items.summary: Git-based hosting for web apps plus tools to add sign-in, data, and storage.
items.details: Amplify lets front-end and mobile developers build and host apps quickly, with Git-based deployments, authentication (using Cognito), APIs, and storage, without deep AWS knowledge.
items.example: A developer connects a React app’s Git repository and gets a hosted site that redeploys on every commit.
items.tip: Front-end or mobile developers building and hosting apps quickly → Amplify.

sections.title: AWS IoT Core
sections.summary: Connect IoT devices securely and route their messages to AWS services.

items.name: Connect IoT devices
items.summary: Devices connect securely (MQTT or HTTPS); rules route their data to other AWS services.
items.details: IoT Core manages device connections, authentication, and messaging. Its rules engine sends device data to services such as Lambda, DynamoDB, or Kinesis.
items.example: Smart thermostats send temperature readings that are stored and analyzed in AWS.
items.tip: Connect and manage IoT devices → AWS IoT Core.

sections.title: Amazon SageMaker AI
sections.summary: Build, train, and deploy your own machine learning models on fully managed infrastructure.

items.name: Custom ML models
items.summary: Managed tools to prepare data, train, tune, deploy, and monitor ML models.
items.details: SageMaker AI is for data scientists and developers who build their own models. It provides notebooks, managed training, hyperparameter tuning, hosting for predictions, and no-code options such as SageMaker Canvas.
items.example: A bank trains a custom fraud-detection model on its own transaction history.
items.tip: Build and train your own models → SageMaker AI. Ready-made AI for a common task → an AI service such as Rekognition.

sections.title: Pre-trained AI services
sections.summary: Add intelligence to applications through an API, with no ML expertise needed.

items.name: Amazon Comprehend
items.summary: Natural language processing: sentiment, entities, key phrases, language, and PII in text.
items.details: Comprehend uses pre-trained models to find insights in text without ML expertise, and can be trained on your own categories.
items.example: A retailer measures customer sentiment across thousands of product reviews.
items.tip: Insights from text → Comprehend.

items.name: Amazon Lex
items.summary: Build voice and text chatbots that understand what users want (intents).
items.details: Lex provides speech recognition and natural language understanding for conversational bots, and integrates with Amazon Connect for contact centers.
items.example: A bank’s phone line lets customers check their balance by speaking.
items.tip: Chatbot or voice bot → Lex.

items.name: Amazon Polly
items.summary: Turns text into lifelike speech in many voices and languages.
items.details: Polly converts text into natural-sounding audio for applications, e-learning, and accessibility features.
items.example: A news app reads articles aloud to its users.
items.tip: Text → speech: Polly.

items.name: Amazon Rekognition
items.summary: Image and video analysis: objects, faces, text in scenes, and unsafe content.
items.details: Rekognition detects labels, faces, and text in images and video, compares faces, and flags inappropriate content.
items.example: A photo-sharing app flags unsafe uploads automatically.
items.tip: Images or video → Rekognition.

items.name: Amazon Textract
items.summary: Extracts text, forms, and tables from scanned documents.
items.details: Textract goes beyond basic OCR by understanding the structure of forms and tables and returning key-value pairs.
items.example: An insurer pulls claim numbers and amounts from scanned claim forms.
items.tip: Text and data from documents → Textract.

items.name: Amazon Transcribe
items.summary: Converts speech to text, with speaker labels and custom vocabularies.
items.details: Transcribe turns speech in audio and video files or live streams into text in many languages.
items.example: A contact center makes its call recordings searchable.
items.tip: Speech → text: Transcribe.

items.name: Amazon Translate
items.summary: Neural machine translation between languages.
items.details: Translate converts text between languages in real time or in batches.
items.example: A help site shows its articles in 10 languages.
items.tip: Translate text → Translate.

items.name: Amazon Q
items.summary: Generative AI assistants: Q Developer for developers; Q Business closed to new customers in July 2026.
items.details: Amazon Q Developer helps developers write, explain, and upgrade code and work with AWS. Amazon Q Business answers employees’ questions from company data; it closed to new customers on 30 July 2026, and Amazon Quick is its successor. The exam guide still lists Amazon Q.
items.example: A developer asks an assistant in the IDE to explain and upgrade old Java code.
items.tip: Generative AI assistant for developers or employees → Amazon Q (new business users get Amazon Quick).

sections.title: AWS Auto Scaling and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling
sections.summary: Automatically add or remove capacity to match demand (elasticity).

items.name: Elasticity
items.summary: Scale out when demand rises and in when it falls, so you pay only for what you need.
items.details: EC2 Auto Scaling groups keep a minimum number of healthy instances and add or remove instances based on policies, such as a target CPU level. AWS Auto Scaling extends scaling to resources such as DynamoDB tables and ECS services.
items.example: An online store grows from 2 to 20 instances during a flash sale and shrinks afterward.
items.tip: Elasticity, matching capacity to demand → Auto Scaling.

items.name: Self-healing and high availability
items.summary: Spreads instances across AZs and replaces unhealthy instances automatically.
items.details: With a load balancer and instances in several Availability Zones, an Auto Scaling group keeps an application running when an instance or an AZ fails.
items.example: When an instance fails its health check, Auto Scaling launches a replacement.
items.tip: High availability = multiple AZs + load balancer + Auto Scaling.

sections.title: AWS CloudFormation
sections.summary: Infrastructure as code: define AWS resources in templates and deploy them as stacks.

items.name: Infrastructure as code
items.summary: Describe resources in JSON or YAML templates; CloudFormation creates, updates, and deletes them together.
items.details: A template defines resources such as VPCs, instances, and databases. Deploying it creates a stack, and changing the template updates the stack in a controlled way. Environments become repeatable and reviewable.
items.example: A company creates identical dev, test, and production environments from one template.
items.tip: Repeatable, version-controlled infrastructure → CloudFormation.

sections.title: AWS CloudTrail
sections.summary: Records API calls and account activity: who did what, when, and from where.

items.name: API activity audit
items.summary: Logs actions taken by users, roles, and AWS services in your account.
items.details: CloudTrail records management events, such as creating or deleting resources, and the event history shows the last 90 days. A trail delivers logs to S3 for long-term retention and analysis.
items.example: An auditor finds which IAM user deleted an S3 bucket last week.
items.tip: Who did what, and when → CloudTrail.

sections.title: Amazon CloudWatch
sections.summary: Monitoring: metrics, logs, alarms, and dashboards for AWS resources and applications.

items.name: Metrics, alarms, and dashboards
items.summary: Track performance metrics and trigger alarms that notify people or take actions.
items.details: CloudWatch collects metrics such as CPU utilization, stores logs, and displays dashboards. Alarms can send SNS notifications or trigger Auto Scaling actions.
items.example: An alarm emails the team when an instance’s CPU stays above 80% for 10 minutes.
items.tip: Performance monitoring and alarms → CloudWatch. API audit trail → CloudTrail.

items.name: CloudWatch Logs
items.summary: Collect, store, and search application and system logs in one place.
items.details: Applications, Lambda functions, and agents send logs to CloudWatch Logs, where you can search them, set retention, and create metrics from log patterns.
items.example: A developer searches Lambda logs to find the cause of an error.

sections.title: AWS Compute Optimizer
sections.summary: Recommends better sizes for EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes, Lambda, and more.

items.name: Rightsizing recommendations
items.summary: Uses utilization history and ML to find over- and under-provisioned resources.
items.details: Compute Optimizer analyzes metrics and recommends instance types, EBS volume types, or Lambda memory sizes that cut cost or improve performance.
items.example: It recommends moving several underused instances to a smaller size.
items.tip: Rightsizing recommendations → Compute Optimizer.

sections.title: AWS Config
sections.summary: Records resource configurations over time and checks them against rules for compliance.

items.name: Configuration history and compliance
items.summary: See how a resource was configured at any time and flag resources that break your rules.
items.details: Config continuously records configuration changes and relationships between resources. Config rules check settings, such as whether S3 buckets block public access, and can trigger automatic remediation.
items.example: An auditor confirms that every EBS volume created since January is encrypted.
items.tip: How a resource’s configuration changed, and whether it complies → Config.

sections.title: AWS Control Tower
sections.summary: Set up and govern a secure multi-account environment (a landing zone) based on best practices.

items.name: Landing zone
items.summary: Automates multi-account setup with Organizations, controls (guardrails), and central logging.
items.details: Control Tower builds a well-architected multi-account environment and applies preventive and detective controls across accounts, using Organizations, IAM Identity Center, and other services behind the scenes.
items.example: A company sets up separate accounts for security, logging, and each team, with standard guardrails.
items.tip: Quickly set up a governed multi-account environment → Control Tower. Manage accounts and SCPs directly → Organizations.

sections.title: AWS Health Dashboard
sections.summary: Shows the health of AWS services and events that affect your account’s resources.

items.name: Service and account health
items.summary: A public view of service status plus a personalized view of events, such as scheduled maintenance.
items.details: The AWS Health Dashboard shows the general status of AWS services. Your account view lists events that affect your resources, such as scheduled maintenance or an EC2 instance retirement, with guidance. The AWS Health API provides programmatic access.
items.example: An engineer sees that an instance is scheduled for retirement and plans to move the workload.
items.tip: Is an AWS issue affecting my resources? → AWS Health Dashboard.

sections.title: AWS License Manager
sections.summary: Track and control software licenses (BYOL) from vendors such as Microsoft and Oracle.

items.name: License tracking
items.summary: Define license rules and enforce limits to stay compliant when you bring your own licenses.
items.details: License Manager tracks license use across AWS and on premises and can block launches that would exceed your entitlements, which makes bring-your-own-license (BYOL) easier.
items.example: A company tracks its SQL Server licenses on EC2 to avoid audit penalties.
items.tip: Manage software licenses and BYOL compliance → License Manager.

sections.title: AWS Management Console
sections.summary: Web interface to access and manage AWS services, plus the AWS Console Mobile Application.

items.name: Web-based access
items.summary: Point-and-click management, best for exploring and one-time tasks.
items.details: The console is a browser interface for creating and managing resources. It is easiest for learning and one-off actions; repeated tasks are better automated with the CLI, SDKs, or infrastructure as code.
items.example: A new user launches their first EC2 instance from the console.

sections.title: AWS Organizations
sections.summary: Manage many AWS accounts centrally: consolidated billing, OUs, and service control policies.

items.name: Multi-account management
items.summary: Group accounts into organizational units (OUs) and apply policies centrally.
items.details: Organizations lets you create and manage accounts, group them into organizational units, and apply policies across them from a management account.
items.example: A company separates production and development workloads into different accounts and OUs.

items.name: Service control policies (SCPs)
items.summary: Set the maximum permissions for accounts in an organization; SCPs don’t grant access.
items.details: An SCP limits what IAM users and roles in member accounts can do, including administrators. For example, an SCP can deny the use of Regions that the company hasn’t approved.
items.example: An SCP blocks every action outside two approved Regions.
items.tip: Restrict what whole accounts can do → SCPs. Grant permissions to identities → IAM policies.

items.name: Consolidated billing
items.summary: One bill for all accounts, with combined usage for volume discounts and shared RIs and Savings Plans.
items.details: The management account pays for all member accounts. Usage is combined for tiered pricing, and Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discounts can be shared across accounts.
items.example: Combined S3 usage across 10 accounts reaches a cheaper pricing tier.
items.tip: One bill plus volume discounts across accounts → consolidated billing in Organizations.

sections.title: AWS Service Catalog
sections.summary: Create and share catalogs of approved IT products that users can launch themselves.

items.name: Approved products
items.summary: Admins publish approved, CloudFormation-based products; users launch them on their own.
items.details: Service Catalog lets central IT define approved configurations, such as a standard web server, and share them, so users deploy only compliant resources without needing broad permissions.
items.example: Developers launch a pre-approved database configuration from a catalog.
items.tip: Let users deploy only approved, standardized resources → Service Catalog.

sections.title: Service Quotas
sections.summary: View and manage the quotas (limits) for AWS services in each account and Region.

items.name: Quota management
items.summary: See current limits and request increases from one place.
items.details: Every AWS service has quotas, such as the number of VPCs per Region. Service Quotas shows them, lets you request increases, and supports CloudWatch alarms as usage approaches a limit.
items.example: Before a big launch, a team requests a higher EC2 vCPU limit.
items.tip: View or raise service limits → Service Quotas.

sections.title: AWS Systems Manager
sections.summary: Operations hub to view, patch, and manage EC2 and on-premises servers at scale.

items.name: Fleet management
items.summary: Patch, configure, and run commands across many servers from one place.
items.details: Systems Manager includes Patch Manager for OS patching, Run Command for scripts across fleets, Session Manager for shell access, and Inventory.
items.example: An admin patches 200 instances in one Patch Manager maintenance window.
items.tip: Manage and patch fleets of servers → Systems Manager.

items.name: Parameter Store
items.summary: Secure, hierarchical storage for configuration data and secrets.
items.details: Parameter Store keeps configuration values and SecureString parameters encrypted with KMS. Unlike Secrets Manager, it doesn’t rotate secrets automatically, and standard parameters cost nothing.
items.example: An app reads its database endpoint and feature flags from Parameter Store.
items.tip: Automatic secret rotation → Secrets Manager. Simple configuration values → Parameter Store.

items.name: Session Manager
items.summary: Shell access to instances without SSH keys, bastion hosts, or open inbound ports.
items.details: Session Manager connects through the Systems Manager agent, is controlled with IAM, and can log every session.
items.example: An engineer opens a shell on a private instance from the console without a bastion host.

sections.title: AWS Trusted Advisor
sections.summary: Automated best-practice checks for cost, security, fault tolerance, performance, quotas, and operations.

items.name: Best-practice checks
items.summary: Inspects your account and recommends improvements, such as removing idle resources or closing open ports.
items.details: Trusted Advisor checks categories including cost optimization, security, fault tolerance, performance, service limits, and operational excellence. Basic Support includes core checks; Business Support+ and higher plans include all checks.
items.example: It flags an S3 bucket with open access and EC2 instances with very low utilization.
items.tip: Account-wide recommendations to save money and improve security → Trusted Advisor.

sections.title: AWS Well-Architected Tool
sections.summary: Review a workload against the Well-Architected Framework and track improvements.

items.name: Workload reviews
items.summary: Answer questions about a workload to find high-risk issues and get an improvement plan.
items.details: The tool walks through questions for each pillar of the Well-Architected Framework, highlights risks, and links to guidance. Lenses add questions for specific types of workload.
items.example: A team reviews its e-commerce workload before launch and fixes two high-risk issues.
items.tip: Review one workload’s architecture → Well-Architected Tool. Automated account-wide checks → Trusted Advisor.

sections.title: AWS Application Discovery Service
sections.summary: Collects data about on-premises servers to plan a migration; closed to new customers since November 2025.

items.name: Discover on-premises servers
items.summary: Gathers server specifications, utilization, and dependencies to plan migration waves.
items.details: Application Discovery Service uses agents or agentless collectors to gather configuration, usage, and network dependency data about on-premises servers. It stopped accepting new customers on 7 November 2025, and AWS Transform now provides similar capabilities, but the exam guide still lists it.
items.example: A company maps which servers talk to each other before deciding what to move together.
items.tip: Discover on-premises inventory and dependencies → Application Discovery Service.

sections.title: AWS Application Migration Service
sections.summary: Lift-and-shift (rehost) servers to AWS with continuous replication and minimal downtime.

items.name: Rehost servers
items.summary: Replicates on-premises or other cloud servers to AWS and launches them as EC2 instances.
items.details: Application Migration Service (AWS MGN) continuously replicates the disks of source servers to AWS. At cutover it launches them on EC2 with minimal downtime and no application changes.
items.example: A company rehosts 50 VMware virtual machines to EC2 with a weekend cutover.
items.tip: Rehost (lift and shift) servers → Application Migration Service.

sections.title: AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS)
sections.summary: Migrate databases to AWS with minimal downtime while the source stays operational.

items.name: Database migration
items.summary: Copies data between databases and keeps replicating changes until cutover.
items.details: DMS migrates data between the same engines (for example Oracle to Oracle) or different engines (for example Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL). The source database keeps running during the migration, and ongoing changes are replicated.
items.example: A retailer moves its SQL Server database to RDS while its online store stays open.
items.tip: Move database data with minimal downtime → DMS.

sections.title: AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT)
sections.summary: Converts database schemas and code from one engine to another for heterogeneous migrations.

items.name: Schema conversion
items.summary: Converts tables, views, and stored procedures, for example from Oracle to PostgreSQL.
items.details: When a migration changes the database engine, SCT converts the schema and code objects, and DMS then moves the data. DMS Schema Conversion offers similar conversion inside DMS.
items.example: A company converts Oracle stored procedures for Aurora PostgreSQL before moving the data with DMS.
items.tip: Changing engines (heterogeneous) → SCT for the schema + DMS for the data.

sections.title: Migration Evaluator
sections.summary: Builds a data-driven business case for moving to AWS, with projected costs.

items.name: Migration business case
items.summary: Analyzes your current on-premises footprint to estimate AWS costs and savings.
items.details: Migration Evaluator collects data about current usage and models the cost of running the same workloads on AWS, including licensing options.
items.example: A finance director gets a projected cost comparison before approving a data center exit.
items.tip: Business case or total cost of ownership (TCO) for migrating → Migration Evaluator.

sections.title: AWS Migration Hub
sections.summary: A central place to track application migrations across AWS migration tools.

items.name: Track migrations
items.summary: One dashboard for the status of migrations that run in several tools.
items.details: Migration Hub shows migration progress across services such as Application Migration Service and DMS. It stopped accepting new customers on 7 November 2025, and AWS Transform now provides these capabilities, but the exam guide still lists Migration Hub.
items.example: A program manager tracks which applications have moved in each migration wave.
items.tip: Track migration progress in one place → Migration Hub.

sections.title: Amazon VPC
sections.summary: Your own logically isolated network in AWS: subnets, route tables, gateways, and firewalls.

items.name: Public and private subnets
items.summary: A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway; a private subnet doesn’t.
items.details: A VPC spans all Availability Zones in a Region, and each subnet lives in one AZ. Public subnets hold internet-facing resources such as load balancers; private subnets hold databases and application servers that shouldn’t be reachable from the internet.
items.example: Web servers run in public subnets and the database runs in private subnets.
items.tip: Each subnet is in exactly one Availability Zone.

items.name: Internet gateway and NAT gateway
items.summary: An internet gateway allows two-way internet access; a NAT gateway lets private subnets reach out only.
items.details: An internet gateway connects a VPC to the internet. A NAT gateway in a public subnet lets instances in private subnets start outbound connections, for example to download patches, while blocking connections that start from the internet.
items.example: Private application servers download operating system updates through a NAT gateway.
items.tip: Private instances need outbound-only internet access → NAT gateway.

items.name: Security groups vs network ACLs
items.summary: Security groups: stateful, instance-level, allow rules only. Network ACLs: stateless, subnet-level, allow and deny.
items.details: A security group is a virtual firewall for an instance. It has only allow rules, and return traffic is allowed automatically (stateful). A network ACL filters traffic entering and leaving a subnet; it has numbered allow and deny rules, and return traffic must be allowed explicitly (stateless).
items.example: A network ACL denies a malicious IP range for a whole subnet, while security groups allow only HTTPS to the web servers.
items.tip: Block a specific IP address → network ACL (security groups can’t deny).

items.name: VPC peering
items.summary: A private connection between two VPCs, including across accounts and Regions.
items.details: Peered VPCs route traffic to each other using private IP addresses. Peering isn’t transitive, so connecting many VPCs is simpler with AWS Transit Gateway.
items.example: A shared-services VPC is peered with an application VPC in another account.
items.tip: Many VPCs and on-premises networks through one hub → Transit Gateway.

sections.title: Amazon Route 53
sections.summary: Highly available DNS, domain registration, health checks, and traffic routing.

items.name: DNS and domains
items.summary: Register domains and translate names such as example.com into IP addresses.
items.details: Route 53 is AWS’s DNS service. It answers DNS queries for your domains, can register domain names, and runs health checks on endpoints.
items.example: A company registers its domain and points it at its load balancer.
items.tip: DNS or domain registration → Route 53.

items.name: Routing policies
items.summary: Route users by latency, location, weight, or health-based failover.
items.details: Routing policies include simple, weighted (split traffic by percentage), latency-based (send users to the lowest-latency Region), geolocation (by where users are), and failover (switch to a standby when health checks fail).
items.example: Users in Europe are sent to the European deployment by latency-based routing.
items.tip: DNS-level failover to a standby site → Route 53 failover routing.

sections.title: Amazon CloudFront
sections.summary: Content delivery network (CDN) that caches content at edge locations close to users.

items.name: Content delivery at the edge
items.summary: Caches static and dynamic content at edge locations to reduce latency for users worldwide.
items.details: CloudFront serves content from hundreds of edge locations, so users get files from a nearby location instead of the origin. It also provides HTTPS, AWS Shield Standard protection, and integration with AWS WAF.
items.example: A video site serves media stored in S3 to viewers worldwide through CloudFront.
items.tip: Speed up delivery of web content to users around the world → CloudFront.

sections.title: AWS Global Accelerator
sections.summary: Routes user traffic over the AWS global network to the best healthy endpoint, using static IP addresses.

items.name: Network-level acceleration
items.summary: Two static anycast IP addresses send TCP and UDP traffic over AWS’s network to healthy endpoints.
items.details: Global Accelerator brings traffic onto the AWS network at the nearest edge location and fails over between Regions quickly. It improves performance for HTTP and non-HTTP applications but, unlike CloudFront, doesn’t cache content.
items.example: A multiplayer game uses Global Accelerator to lower latency for UDP traffic worldwide.
items.tip: Caching web content → CloudFront. Static IPs and fast failover for TCP/UDP apps → Global Accelerator.

sections.title: AWS Direct Connect
sections.summary: Dedicated private network connection from your premises to AWS.

items.name: Dedicated connection
items.summary: Consistent, private bandwidth that doesn’t travel over the public internet.
items.details: Direct Connect links your data center to AWS through a dedicated line at a Direct Connect location. It gives consistent performance and can lower data transfer costs for large volumes, but it takes weeks to set up.
items.example: A bank sends terabytes of trading data to AWS every day over a dedicated 10 Gbps connection.
items.tip: Consistent performance over a private dedicated link → Direct Connect. Quick encrypted connection over the internet → Site-to-Site VPN.

sections.title: AWS VPN: AWS Site-to-Site VPN and AWS Client VPN
sections.summary: Encrypted connections over the internet, network-to-network or user-to-network.

items.name: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
items.summary: Encrypted IPsec tunnels between your on-premises network and AWS over the internet.
items.details: Site-to-Site VPN is quick to set up and inexpensive. Because it uses the internet, performance can vary, so it is often used on its own for smaller needs or as a backup for Direct Connect.
items.example: A branch office connects to its VPC in an afternoon.
items.tip: Fast, low-cost, encrypted hybrid connection → Site-to-Site VPN.

items.name: AWS Client VPN
items.summary: Managed VPN that lets individual users connect securely from their own devices.
items.details: Client VPN gives remote employees encrypted access to resources in AWS and on premises using an OpenVPN-based client.
items.example: Remote staff connect to internal applications from home.
items.tip: Individual remote users → Client VPN. Whole networks → Site-to-Site VPN.

sections.title: AWS Transit Gateway
sections.summary: Network hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks.

items.name: Hub-and-spoke networking
items.summary: Attach VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect to one central gateway instead of many peering links.
items.details: Transit Gateway simplifies networks with many VPCs: each network attaches once, and routing is managed in one place.
items.example: A company connects 80 VPCs and two data centers through one transit gateway.
items.tip: Connect many VPCs and on-premises networks simply → Transit Gateway.

sections.title: AWS PrivateLink
sections.summary: Private connectivity from a VPC to AWS services and partner services without using the internet.

items.name: Private access to services
items.summary: Interface VPC endpoints let resources reach services privately over the AWS network.
items.details: With PrivateLink, traffic to supported AWS services, or to services hosted in other accounts, stays on the AWS network, so private subnets need no internet gateway or NAT. Amazon S3 and DynamoDB also offer gateway endpoints.
items.example: Instances in a private subnet call an AWS service through an interface endpoint without internet access.
items.tip: Access services privately without crossing the internet → PrivateLink (VPC endpoints).

sections.title: Amazon API Gateway
sections.summary: Create, publish, secure, and monitor APIs at any scale, often in front of Lambda.

items.name: Managed APIs
items.summary: A front door for applications that handles requests, authorization, throttling, and monitoring.
items.details: API Gateway creates REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs that send requests to Lambda functions, containers, or other backends, with throttling, caching, and authorization built in.
items.example: A mobile app calls an API Gateway endpoint that runs Lambda functions.
items.tip: Create and manage APIs for a serverless backend → API Gateway.

sections.title: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)
sections.summary: Control who can sign in (authentication) and what they can do (authorization) in an AWS account.

items.name: Users, groups, and roles
items.summary: Users have long-term credentials; groups collect users; roles provide temporary credentials.
items.details: An IAM user represents a person or application. A group lets you attach permissions to many users at once. A role is assumed by users, AWS services, or other accounts to get temporary credentials, with no long-term keys to manage.
items.example: An EC2 instance uses a role to read from S3 instead of storing access keys.
items.tip: Applications running on AWS → IAM roles, not access keys.

items.name: Policies and least privilege
items.summary: JSON policies allow or deny actions on resources; grant only what is needed.
items.details: Identity-based policies attach to users, groups, and roles; resource-based policies attach to resources such as S3 buckets. AWS managed policies are prebuilt; customer managed policies are your own reusable policies. An explicit deny always overrides an allow.
items.example: A support group gets a custom policy that allows read-only access to EC2.
items.tip: Start with the minimum permissions and add more only when needed.

items.name: MFA and password policies
items.summary: Add a second factor to sign-ins and enforce strong passwords for IAM users.
items.details: Multi-factor authentication requires a code or a security key in addition to a password. An account password policy sets length, complexity, and expiration rules for IAM users.
items.example: A company requires MFA for all console users and a 14-character minimum password.
items.tip: Most effective protection for sign-ins → MFA.

items.name: Access keys
items.summary: Long-term credentials for programmatic access; avoid them where possible and rotate them.
items.details: Access keys (an access key ID and a secret) let users call AWS from the CLI or SDKs. Best practice is to prefer temporary credentials from roles or IAM Identity Center, never share keys or put them in code, and rotate or delete unused keys.
items.example: A developer accidentally publishes keys in a public code repository, so the keys must be deactivated at once.
items.tip: Never create access keys for the root user.

items.name: Credential report and IAM Access Analyzer
items.summary: Find users without MFA or with old keys, and resources shared outside your account.
items.details: The credential report lists every IAM user with the status of their passwords, access keys, and MFA. IAM Access Analyzer identifies resources shared with external principals and unused access, helping you move toward least privilege.
items.example: An auditor downloads the credential report to find users without MFA.
items.tip: Which users lack MFA or have old keys? → credential report.

sections.title: AWS IAM Identity Center
sections.summary: Single sign-on to multiple AWS accounts and business applications with one set of credentials.

items.name: Workforce single sign-on
items.summary: Employees sign in once and open their assigned AWS accounts and apps with temporary credentials.
items.details: IAM Identity Center (successor to AWS Single Sign-On) is the recommended way to manage workforce access to multiple accounts in AWS Organizations. It can use its own directory or an external identity provider such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta.
items.example: Employees sign in with their corporate credentials and choose which AWS account to open.
items.tip: Workforce access to many AWS accounts with single sign-on → IAM Identity Center.

sections.title: Amazon Cognito
sections.summary: Sign-up, sign-in, and access control for the users of your web and mobile apps.

items.name: Customer identity for apps
items.summary: User pools handle sign-up and sign-in; identity pools give app users temporary AWS credentials.
items.details: Cognito manages your application’s end users, not your employees. It supports social sign-in (such as Google and Apple) and enterprise federation, and scales to millions of users.
items.example: A shopping app lets customers sign in with their Google account.
items.tip: Users of your app → Cognito. Employees accessing AWS accounts → IAM Identity Center.

sections.title: AWS Directory Service
sections.summary: Managed Microsoft Active Directory in AWS, or a connection to your on-premises AD.

items.name: Managed Active Directory
items.summary: Run Microsoft AD as a managed service, or connect AWS to an existing directory.
items.details: AWS Managed Microsoft AD lets AD-aware applications and services, such as WorkSpaces and FSx for Windows File Server, use Active Directory without you running domain controllers. AD Connector forwards sign-in requests to an on-premises AD.
items.example: WorkSpaces users sign in with their existing corporate Active Directory credentials.
items.tip: Microsoft Active Directory in AWS → Directory Service.

sections.title: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS)
sections.summary: Create and control the encryption keys used to encrypt data across AWS services.

items.name: Managed encryption keys
items.summary: Integrated with most AWS services for encryption at rest; every use of a key is logged in CloudTrail.
items.details: KMS creates and protects keys in hardware security modules that AWS manages. Services such as S3, EBS, and RDS use KMS keys to encrypt data at rest. Customer managed keys let you control the key policy, rotation, and disabling of a key.
items.example: A company encrypts its S3 buckets and EBS volumes with its own customer managed key.
items.tip: Create and manage encryption keys → KMS. Dedicated single-tenant HSMs → CloudHSM.

sections.title: AWS CloudHSM
sections.summary: Dedicated, single-tenant hardware security modules (HSMs) in the AWS Cloud.

items.name: Dedicated HSMs
items.summary: You alone control the keys in FIPS-validated hardware that only your account uses.
items.details: CloudHSM gives you HSMs dedicated to your account. AWS manages the hardware, but you manage the keys and HSM users, which some regulations require.
items.example: A payment processor must keep its keys in single-tenant HSMs under its own control.
items.tip: Regulations require dedicated hardware and full control of keys → CloudHSM.

sections.title: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
sections.summary: Provision and automatically renew SSL/TLS certificates for encryption in transit.

items.name: SSL/TLS certificates
items.summary: Free public certificates for load balancers and CloudFront, renewed automatically.
items.details: ACM issues and manages the certificates that enable HTTPS. Public certificates used with integrated services such as Elastic Load Balancing and CloudFront are free and renew automatically.
items.example: A website enables HTTPS on its load balancer with an ACM certificate.
items.tip: Encryption in transit with SSL/TLS certificates → ACM.

sections.title: AWS Secrets Manager
sections.summary: Store, retrieve, and automatically rotate secrets such as database passwords and API keys.

items.name: Secrets with rotation
items.summary: Applications fetch secrets at run time instead of hardcoding them; rotation can be automatic.
items.details: Secrets Manager encrypts secrets with KMS, controls access with IAM, and can rotate database credentials automatically on a schedule.
items.example: An app reads its RDS password from Secrets Manager, which rotates it every 30 days.
items.tip: Automatic rotation of credentials → Secrets Manager.

sections.title: Amazon GuardDuty
sections.summary: Intelligent threat detection that monitors accounts and workloads for malicious activity.

items.name: Threat detection
items.summary: Analyzes CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and more to detect threats such as compromised credentials.
items.details: GuardDuty uses machine learning and threat intelligence to detect suspicious activity, such as cryptocurrency mining or contact with known malicious IP addresses, without installing agents. Findings can trigger automated responses.
items.example: GuardDuty reports that an instance is communicating with a known malware server.
items.tip: Detect threats and malicious activity → GuardDuty.

sections.title: Amazon Inspector
sections.summary: Automated vulnerability management for EC2 instances, container images, and Lambda functions.

items.name: Vulnerability scanning
items.summary: Continuously scans workloads for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure.
items.details: Inspector discovers workloads automatically, checks them for known software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and network reachability, and prioritizes findings by risk.
items.example: Inspector flags a container image that uses a library with a critical vulnerability.
items.tip: Software vulnerabilities in EC2, containers, or Lambda → Inspector.

sections.title: Amazon Macie
sections.summary: Discovers and helps protect sensitive data, such as PII, in Amazon S3 using machine learning.

items.name: Sensitive data discovery
items.summary: Finds PII and other sensitive data in S3 buckets and reports bucket security risks.
items.details: Macie scans S3 objects for sensitive data such as names, credit card numbers, and credentials, and evaluates bucket settings such as public access.
items.example: Macie finds passport numbers in a bucket that was thought to contain only logs.
items.tip: Find PII or sensitive data in S3 → Macie.

sections.title: Amazon Detective
sections.summary: Analyze and visualize security data to investigate the root cause of findings.

items.name: Security investigations
items.summary: Builds a graph from log data so analysts can investigate GuardDuty findings and suspicious activity.
items.details: Detective automatically collects log data and organizes it into visualizations that show how resources, users, and IP addresses interacted over time, which speeds up investigations.
items.example: An analyst traces how a compromised access key was used over several days.
items.tip: Detect threats → GuardDuty. Investigate the root cause → Detective.

sections.title: AWS Security Hub
sections.summary: A central view of security findings and automated best-practice checks across accounts.

items.name: Security posture in one place
items.summary: Aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and partner tools, and runs compliance checks.
items.details: Security Hub collects and prioritizes findings from AWS security services and partner tools and runs automated checks against standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices and the CIS benchmarks.
items.example: A security team sees findings from all its accounts in one dashboard.
items.tip: One dashboard for security findings and compliance checks → Security Hub.

sections.title: AWS Shield
sections.summary: Managed DDoS protection: Shield Standard is automatic and free; Shield Advanced adds more protection.

items.name: Shield Standard
items.summary: Automatic protection against common network and transport layer DDoS attacks, at no extra cost.
items.details: Every AWS customer gets Shield Standard, which protects against the most common infrastructure DDoS attacks on services such as CloudFront and Route 53.
items.example: A website on CloudFront is protected from a SYN flood with no setup.

items.name: Shield Advanced
