items.summary: Paid protection with enhanced detection, the Shield Response Team, and DDoS cost protection.
items.details: Shield Advanced protects EC2, load balancers, CloudFront, Global Accelerator, and Route 53, with 24/7 access to the Shield Response Team and credits for scaling charges caused by an attack.
items.example: A gaming company that is attacked frequently subscribes to Shield Advanced.
items.tip: DDoS protection → Shield. Web exploits such as SQL injection → WAF.

sections.title: AWS WAF
sections.summary: Web application firewall that filters HTTP(S) requests to protect against common web exploits.

items.name: Web application firewall
items.summary: Rules block attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, or traffic from specific IPs or countries.
items.details: AWS WAF works with CloudFront, Application Load Balancers, and API Gateway. You use managed rule groups or write your own rules, including rate limits.
items.example: A rule blocks requests that contain SQL injection patterns before they reach the application.
items.tip: Protect a web application from layer 7 attacks → WAF.

sections.title: AWS Firewall Manager
sections.summary: Centrally configure and manage firewall rules across the accounts in AWS Organizations.

items.name: Central firewall management
items.summary: Apply WAF rules, Shield Advanced, and security group policies across all accounts automatically.
items.details: Firewall Manager enforces security policies consistently, including for accounts and resources added later.
items.example: A security team applies the same WAF rules to every load balancer in 40 accounts.
items.tip: Manage WAF and firewall policies across many accounts → Firewall Manager.

sections.title: AWS Artifact
sections.summary: Self-service portal for AWS compliance reports and agreements.

items.name: Compliance reports and agreements
items.summary: Download AWS SOC, ISO, and PCI reports, and review and accept agreements such as the BAA.
items.details: Artifact gives on-demand access to AWS security and compliance documents produced by third-party auditors, which customers use as evidence in their own audits.
items.example: An auditor downloads AWS’s SOC 2 report for a compliance review.
items.tip: AWS compliance reports or agreements → Artifact.

sections.title: AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM)
sections.summary: Securely share AWS resources, such as subnets and transit gateways, with other accounts.

items.name: Share resources across accounts
items.summary: Create a resource once and share it with specific accounts or a whole organization.
items.details: RAM avoids duplicating resources: for example, a central networking account shares subnets or a transit gateway with application accounts.
items.example: A network team shares VPC subnets with every application account in the organization.
items.tip: Share resources across accounts → RAM.

sections.title: AWS Lambda
sections.summary: Run code without provisioning servers; pay per request and for the compute time used.

items.name: Serverless functions
items.summary: Code runs in response to events and scales automatically, with no servers to manage.
items.details: Lambda runs functions when events happen, such as an S3 upload, an API Gateway request, or a schedule. You pay per request and for compute duration, and a single invocation can run for up to 15 minutes.
items.example: When a photo is uploaded to S3, a Lambda function creates a thumbnail.
items.tip: Event-driven code with no servers → Lambda. Long-running processes → EC2 or containers.

sections.title: AWS Fargate
sections.summary: Serverless compute engine for containers on ECS and EKS.

items.name: Serverless containers
items.summary: Run containers without managing EC2 instances; pay for the vCPU and memory used.
items.details: With Fargate you define the container and the CPU and memory it needs, and AWS provisions and scales the compute underneath. There are no servers to patch.
items.example: A team runs its ECS tasks on Fargate so it never manages container hosts.
items.tip: Containers without managing servers → Fargate.

sections.title: Amazon S3
sections.summary: Object storage designed for 11 nines of durability, for any amount of data.

items.name: Object storage
items.summary: Store files as objects in buckets, with virtually unlimited capacity, accessed over HTTPS.
items.details: S3 stores objects (files plus metadata) in buckets and is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability. Common uses include backups, data lakes, static website content, and media.
items.example: A company stores product images in S3 and serves them through CloudFront.
items.tip: Object storage, data lakes, backups, static content → S3.

items.name: S3 storage classes
items.summary: Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, and the Glacier classes.
items.details: Classes trade storage price against access cost and retrieval time. Standard is for frequently accessed data; Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between tiers automatically when access patterns are unknown; Standard-IA and One Zone-IA are for infrequent access (One Zone-IA keeps data in one AZ); Glacier classes are for archives.
items.example: Rarely read compliance archives go to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
items.tip: Unknown or changing access patterns → S3 Intelligent-Tiering.

items.name: Lifecycle rules
items.summary: Automatically move objects to cheaper classes or delete them after a set time.
items.details: Lifecycle rules transition objects, for example to Standard-IA after 30 days and to a Glacier class after 90 days, and can expire old objects or old versions.
items.example: Log files move to Glacier after 90 days and are deleted after 7 years.
items.tip: Data that ages predictably → lifecycle rules.

items.name: Versioning and Block Public Access
items.summary: Versioning keeps every version of an object; Block Public Access prevents accidental public exposure.
items.details: Versioning protects against accidental deletes and overwrites by keeping earlier versions. Block Public Access settings, on by default for new buckets, override any policy that would make data public.
items.example: A user restores a file that was accidentally overwritten.

sections.title: Amazon S3 Glacier storage classes
sections.summary: Low-cost archive storage classes in S3, with retrieval times from milliseconds to hours.

items.name: Archive tiers
items.summary: Glacier Instant Retrieval (milliseconds), Flexible Retrieval (minutes to hours), and Deep Archive (hours, lowest price).
items.details: Glacier classes are for data you rarely access but must keep, such as compliance records and old media. The lower storage price comes with retrieval charges and, for Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive, longer retrieval times.
items.example: A hospital keeps imaging records for 10 years in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
items.tip: Archive needed within milliseconds → Glacier Instant Retrieval. Rarely needed, lowest price → Deep Archive.

sections.title: Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
sections.summary: Block storage volumes for EC2 that persist independently of the instance.

items.name: Block storage for EC2
items.summary: Network-attached volumes used like a hard drive, in a single Availability Zone.
items.details: An EBS volume attaches to an EC2 instance in the same AZ and keeps its data when the instance stops. Volume types range from general purpose SSD to high-performance SSD and low-cost HDD.
items.example: A database server keeps its data on an EBS SSD volume.
items.tip: Persistent block storage for an EC2 instance → EBS.

items.name: EBS snapshots
items.summary: Point-in-time, incremental backups of volumes, stored in S3.
items.details: Snapshots back up a volume incrementally. They can create new volumes in any AZ and can be copied to another Region for disaster recovery.
items.example: Nightly snapshots let a team restore a volume after a bad deployment.

items.name: Instance store vs EBS
items.summary: Instance store is temporary disk on the host; its data is lost when the instance stops.
items.details: Instance store gives very fast local storage at no extra cost, but it is temporary: data disappears when the instance stops, hibernates, or terminates. Use it for caches, buffers, and scratch data.
items.example: A video transcoder uses instance store for temporary files.
items.tip: Temporary, very fast scratch space → instance store. Data that must persist → EBS.

sections.title: Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)
sections.summary: Serverless, elastic shared file storage (NFS) for Linux workloads.

items.name: Shared file system
items.summary: Many instances across AZs mount the same file system; capacity grows and shrinks automatically.
items.details: EFS provides a managed NFS file system that many Linux EC2 instances, containers, and Lambda functions can share. You pay for the storage you use, with infrequent-access classes for colder files.
items.example: A fleet of web servers shares one directory of uploaded content.
items.tip: Shared Linux file storage across many instances → EFS.

sections.title: Amazon FSx
sections.summary: Fully managed file systems such as Windows File Server, NetApp ONTAP, and OpenZFS.

items.name: Managed file systems
items.summary: Choose a file system built for the workload, such as Windows SMB shares joined to Active Directory.
items.details: FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB file shares integrated with Active Directory for Windows applications. FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS bring familiar enterprise storage features. (FSx for Lustre, for high-performance computing, is out of scope for CLF-C02.)
items.example: A company moves its Windows file shares to FSx for Windows File Server.
items.tip: Windows file shares (SMB) → FSx for Windows File Server. Linux NFS shares → EFS.

sections.title: AWS Storage Gateway
sections.summary: Hybrid storage that gives on-premises applications access to cloud storage, with local caching.

items.name: Hybrid cloud storage
items.summary: File, volume, and tape gateways connect on-premises applications to S3 and other AWS storage.
items.details: Storage Gateway runs on premises as a virtual machine or appliance. S3 File Gateway presents S3 as file shares with a local cache, and Tape Gateway replaces physical backup tapes with virtual tapes stored in S3 Glacier.
items.example: An office keeps a local cache of frequently used files while all data is stored in S3.
items.tip: On-premises access to cloud storage with a local cache (hybrid) → Storage Gateway.

sections.title: AWS Backup
sections.summary: Centrally manage and automate backups across AWS services and accounts.

items.name: Central backup management
items.summary: Backup plans schedule and retain backups of EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, S3, and more.
items.details: AWS Backup applies policy-based backup plans with schedules and retention periods, can copy backups across Regions and accounts, and helps meet compliance requirements from one place.
items.example: A company backs up all production databases daily and keeps each copy for 35 days.
items.tip: Centralized, policy-based backups across services → AWS Backup.

sections.title: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery
sections.summary: Recover on-premises and cloud servers into AWS quickly, using continuous replication.

items.name: Disaster recovery for servers
items.summary: Replicates servers continuously to low-cost staging and launches them in AWS during a disaster.
items.details: Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS) keeps block-level replicas of source servers. In a disaster it launches recovery instances within minutes, with recovery points measured in seconds.
items.example: A company fails over its on-premises ERP servers to AWS when its data center loses power.
items.tip: Disaster recovery of servers into AWS → Elastic Disaster Recovery. Scheduled backups → AWS Backup.

sections.title: Benefits of the AWS Cloud
sections.summary: The value proposition of the cloud (task 1.1).

items.name: The six advantages of cloud computing
items.summary: Variable expense, economies of scale, no capacity guessing, agility, no data centers, global in minutes.
items.details: AWS describes six advantages: trade fixed (capital) expense for variable expense; benefit from massive economies of scale; stop guessing capacity; increase speed and agility; stop spending money running and maintaining data centers; and go global in minutes.
items.example: A startup launches on three continents without buying any hardware.
items.tip: Know all six by name; questions often paraphrase one of them.

items.name: Elasticity and scalability
items.summary: Scalability is growing to handle more load; elasticity grows and shrinks automatically with demand.
items.details: A scalable system can handle more load by adding resources. An elastic system adds and removes resources automatically as demand changes, so you don’t pay for idle capacity.
items.example: A ticketing site scales out for a concert sale and back in an hour later.
items.tip: Automatically matching capacity to demand in both directions → elasticity (Auto Scaling).

items.name: Agility and speed
items.summary: Resources are available in minutes, so teams can experiment and deliver faster.
items.details: Because resources can be provisioned in minutes instead of weeks, teams can try ideas cheaply and throw away what doesn’t work. Agility is about the speed of innovation, not raw performance.
items.example: A team creates a test environment for one day and deletes it afterward.

items.name: High availability and fault tolerance
items.summary: Design across multiple Availability Zones so a single failure doesn’t stop the application.
items.details: High availability keeps a system running with minimal downtime; fault tolerance keeps it running without interruption despite component failures. AWS makes both practical with multiple AZs, load balancing, and managed services that replicate data.
items.example: An application in two AZs keeps serving users when one AZ fails.
items.tip: Increase availability → deploy across multiple Availability Zones.

items.name: Global reach and speed of deployment
items.summary: Deploy in Regions around the world in minutes to serve users with low latency.
items.details: With Regions worldwide and hundreds of edge locations, a company can deploy close to its customers quickly, without building data centers.
items.example: A European company launches in Asia by deploying to the Tokyo Region.

sections.title: AWS Well-Architected Framework
sections.summary: Design principles and the six pillars (task 1.2).

items.name: The six pillars
items.summary: Operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability.
items.details: The framework helps you evaluate architectures against best practices in six pillars. Each pillar has design principles and review questions, which the Well-Architected Tool uses.
items.example: A review finds that backups are never tested, a reliability risk.
items.tip: Learn the six pillars with one example each.

items.name: Operational excellence
items.summary: Run and monitor systems well, and continually improve processes and procedures.
items.details: Design principles include performing operations as code, making frequent, small, reversible changes, anticipating failure, and learning from operational events.
items.example: Teams deploy small changes through automated pipelines and review every incident.
items.tip: Operations as code and small reversible changes → operational excellence.

items.name: Security
items.summary: Protect data, systems, and assets with a strong identity foundation, traceability, and defense in depth.
items.details: Design principles include a strong identity foundation (least privilege), enabling traceability (logging and monitoring), applying security at all layers, automating security best practices, and protecting data in transit and at rest.
items.example: Every action is logged, and data is encrypted at rest and in transit.

items.name: Reliability
items.summary: Recover from failure automatically, test recovery, scale horizontally, and stop guessing capacity.
items.details: Design principles include automatically recovering from failure, testing recovery procedures, scaling horizontally to increase availability, stopping guessing capacity, and managing change through automation.
items.example: An application runs in several AZs, and its recovery plan is tested every quarter.
items.tip: Automatic recovery and multi-AZ designs → reliability.

items.name: Performance efficiency
items.summary: Use computing resources efficiently as demand and technology change.
items.details: Design principles include using serverless architectures, going global in minutes, experimenting more often, and choosing the right resource types for each workload.
items.example: A team moves to a newer instance generation that gives more performance per dollar.

items.name: Cost optimization
items.summary: Deliver business value at the lowest price: pay only for what you use and measure efficiency.
items.details: Design principles include adopting a consumption model, measuring overall efficiency, stopping spending money on undifferentiated heavy lifting, and analyzing and attributing expenditure, for example with tags.
items.example: Development instances stop automatically outside working hours.
items.tip: Rightsizing, consumption-based pricing, and cost attribution → cost optimization.

items.name: Sustainability
items.summary: Minimize environmental impact: maximize utilization, use managed services, and reduce waste.
items.details: Design principles include understanding your impact, maximizing utilization, adopting more efficient hardware and software, and using managed services and shared infrastructure.
items.example: A team moves to energy-efficient Graviton instances and deletes data it no longer needs.
items.tip: Reduce energy use and environmental impact → sustainability.

sections.title: AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF)
sections.summary: How organizations plan and run a cloud transformation (task 1.3).

items.name: The six CAF perspectives
items.summary: Business, people, and governance (business); platform, security, and operations (technical).
items.details: AWS CAF groups guidance into six perspectives. Business, people, and governance focus on business capabilities; platform, security, and operations focus on technical capabilities.
items.example: The people perspective covers training staff and changing roles for the cloud.
items.tip: People → culture, skills, and roles. Governance → risk, cost, and program management. Platform → architecture and infrastructure.

items.name: CAF business outcomes
items.summary: Reduced business risk, improved ESG performance, increased revenue, and increased operational efficiency.
items.details: AWS CAF describes the value of cloud adoption as four business outcomes: reduced business risk; improved environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance; increased revenue; and increased operational efficiency.
items.example: Moving to more energy-efficient infrastructure improves a company’s ESG reporting.

items.name: Transformation journey
items.summary: Envision, align, launch, and scale.
items.details: CAF describes an iterative journey: envision how the cloud will accelerate business outcomes, align stakeholders and close capability gaps, launch pilots in production, and scale them across the business.
items.example: A company proves value with one pilot application (launch) before migrating its portfolio (scale).

sections.title: Migration strategies and resources
sections.summary: The 7 Rs and help available for moving to AWS (task 1.3).

items.name: The 7 Rs of migration
items.summary: Retire, retain, rehost, relocate, repurchase, replatform, and refactor.
items.details: Rehost: lift and shift with no changes. Replatform: lift, tinker, and shift, for example to a managed database. Repurchase: move to a different product, often SaaS. Refactor: re-architect for cloud-native features. Relocate: move VMware workloads as they are. Retain: keep as is for now. Retire: switch off what is no longer needed.
items.example: Moving a self-managed database to Amazon RDS without changing the application is replatforming.
items.tip: Lift and shift → rehost. Move to SaaS → repurchase. Re-architect → refactor.

items.name: Database replication during migration
items.summary: Replicate data continuously so cutover is quick and downtime is minimal.
items.details: Tools such as AWS DMS keep the source and target databases in sync while the source stays live, so the final switch takes minutes.
items.example: An online store cuts over to Aurora overnight with only seconds of data lag.

items.name: Migration help
items.summary: AWS Professional Services, AWS Partners, Prescriptive Guidance, and migration tools.
items.details: Help with migrations includes AWS Professional Services, AWS Partners, AWS Prescriptive Guidance, and tools such as Application Discovery Service, Application Migration Service, DMS, and Migration Evaluator.
items.example: A company engages an AWS Partner to plan and run its data center exit.

sections.title: Cloud economics
sections.summary: Costs and savings of moving to the cloud (task 1.4).

items.name: Fixed vs variable costs
items.summary: On premises you buy capacity up front (capital expense); in the cloud you pay as you go (variable).
items.details: With on-premises infrastructure you pay for hardware in advance based on forecasts, even if it sits idle. Cloud costs are variable and follow actual usage.
items.example: A retailer stops buying servers for its peak season and pays for extra capacity only in December.
items.tip: Trade capital expense for variable expense.

items.name: Costs of on-premises environments
items.summary: Hardware, data center space, power, cooling, staff, and maintenance, much of it fixed.
items.details: A total cost of ownership (TCO) comparison includes not only servers but also facilities, power, cooling, networking, hardware refreshes, and the people who run them.
items.example: A migration business case includes power, cooling, and staff costs, not just server prices.

items.name: Licensing: BYOL vs license-included
items.summary: Bring licenses you already own where allowed, or pay for licenses included in the hourly price.
items.details: With license-included pricing, the cost of software such as Windows Server or SQL Server is part of the AWS price. With bring your own license (BYOL), you use licenses you already own, which sometimes requires Dedicated Hosts.
items.example: A company with existing SQL Server licenses uses BYOL on Dedicated Hosts.
items.tip: Licenses counted per physical core or socket → BYOL on Dedicated Hosts.

items.name: Rightsizing
items.summary: Match instance types and sizes to actual needs to avoid paying for unused capacity.
items.details: Monitoring utilization and moving to smaller or better-suited instance types cuts cost without hurting performance. Compute Optimizer and Cost Explorer give recommendations.
items.example: Twenty instances that run at 5% CPU are moved to a smaller size.

items.name: Economies of scale and automation
items.summary: AWS’s scale lowers prices, and automation reduces manual work and errors.
items.details: Because AWS aggregates usage from many customers, it achieves lower costs and passes savings on. Automating provisioning and operations also reduces manual effort and mistakes.
items.example: Infrastructure as code builds a new environment in minutes without manual steps.

sections.title: AWS shared responsibility model
sections.summary: What AWS secures and what the customer secures (task 2.1).

items.name: Security of vs security in the cloud
items.summary: AWS secures the infrastructure; customers secure what they put in the cloud.
items.details: AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: the hardware, software, networking, and facilities that run AWS services. Customers are responsible for security in the cloud: their data, identity and access management, operating system and application configuration, network settings such as security groups, and encryption choices.
items.example: AWS protects the data center; the customer decides who can read an S3 bucket.
items.tip: Physical security, hardware, and the virtualization layer → AWS. Data, IAM, and configuration → customer.

items.name: How responsibility shifts by service
items.summary: The more managed the service, the more AWS handles: EC2 → RDS → Lambda.
items.details: With EC2 (IaaS) the customer patches the guest OS and applications. With RDS, AWS patches the OS and database engine, but the customer manages access and data. With Lambda, AWS manages the servers and runtime; the customer manages the code, permissions, and data.
items.example: A customer must patch the operating system on EC2 but not on RDS.
items.tip: Guest OS patching on EC2 → customer. OS patching for RDS or Lambda → AWS.

items.name: Shared controls
items.summary: Patch management, configuration management, and awareness and training apply to both, each in its own layer.
items.details: AWS patches and configures the infrastructure, and the customer patches and configures its guest operating systems and applications. AWS trains its own staff, and the customer trains its staff.
items.example: Both AWS and the customer must train their employees on security.

sections.title: Security, governance, and compliance concepts
sections.summary: Compliance information, data residency, and logging (task 2.2).

items.name: AWS compliance programs
items.summary: AWS infrastructure is assessed against standards such as SOC, ISO 27001, and PCI DSS.
items.details: AWS maintains certifications and attestations for its infrastructure. Customers inherit these controls but remain responsible for configuring their own workloads in a compliant way. Requirements vary by country, industry, and service.
items.example: A healthcare company uses HIPAA-eligible services and accepts the BAA in AWS Artifact.
items.tip: Where do I get AWS’s compliance reports? → AWS Artifact.

items.name: Data residency
items.summary: Data stays in the Region you choose unless you move it.
items.details: Customers choose the Region where their data is stored, which helps meet data sovereignty laws. AWS doesn’t move customer data out of a Region without the customer’s action.
items.example: A German company keeps customer data in the Frankfurt Region.
items.tip: Data sovereignty requirement → choose the Region.

items.name: Where to capture security logs
items.summary: CloudTrail for API activity, CloudWatch Logs for app and system logs, Config for configuration history.
items.details: Governance relies on logs: CloudTrail records who did what, Config records resource configuration history, CloudWatch collects metrics and logs, and access reports such as the IAM credential report show credential status.
items.example: Logs from all accounts are delivered to a central S3 bucket in a dedicated logging account.

items.name: Encryption at rest and in transit
items.summary: At rest: KMS keys for stored data. In transit: TLS (HTTPS) and VPN.
items.details: Most services that store data, such as S3, EBS, RDS, and DynamoDB, encrypt at rest with KMS keys, and S3 encrypts new objects by default. TLS certificates from ACM enable HTTPS, and Site-to-Site VPN encrypts traffic between networks.
items.example: A website forces HTTPS so login details can’t be read in transit, and its database is encrypted with a KMS key.
items.tip: Keys for data at rest → KMS. HTTPS certificates → ACM.

sections.title: Protecting the AWS account root user
sections.summary: The most powerful identity in an account (task 2.3).

items.name: The root user
items.summary: The identity that created the account, with full access to everything; use it rarely.
items.details: The root user can do anything in the account. Best practice is to enable MFA on it, never create access keys for it, store its credentials securely, and use IAM Identity Center or IAM roles for everyday work.
items.example: An administrator signs in as the root user only to close an old account.
items.tip: Protect the root user: MFA, no access keys, no daily use.

items.name: Tasks only the root user can perform
items.summary: For example: change the root email or password, close the account, and restore IAM admin access.
items.details: Examples include changing account settings such as the account name, root email address, and root password; closing the AWS account; and restoring permissions when the only IAM administrator loses access.
items.example: Only the root user can close an AWS account.
items.tip: Close the account or change the root email → root user.

sections.title: Access management practices
sections.summary: Least privilege, federation, cross-account access, and credential storage (task 2.3).

items.name: Principle of least privilege
items.summary: Grant only the permissions needed for a task, and nothing more.
items.details: Start with minimal permissions and add more only when needed. Group users with the same job, attach managed policies to groups, and review unused permissions regularly with IAM Access Analyzer.
items.example: Interns get read-only access to the test account only.
items.tip: Least privilege limits the damage from mistakes and stolen credentials.

items.name: Federation and identity types
items.summary: Use an existing identity provider so people sign in with their corporate credentials.
items.details: Federation lets users authenticate with an external identity provider (SAML 2.0 or OpenID Connect) and receive temporary AWS credentials. IAM Identity Center is the usual way to federate employees; Cognito federates your app’s users.
items.example: Employees use their Microsoft Entra ID credentials to access AWS accounts.

items.name: Cross-account roles
items.summary: Users in one account assume a role in another account, with no new credentials.
items.details: A role in the target account trusts the source account. Users who are allowed to assume it get temporary credentials for the target account.
items.example: Auditors in a security account assume a read-only role in every production account.

items.name: Storing credentials safely
items.summary: Keep secrets in Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store, never in source code.
items.details: Applications should fetch secrets when they run. Secrets Manager adds automatic rotation; Parameter Store stores configuration values and secure strings.
items.example: A Lambda function reads its API key from Secrets Manager.

sections.title: Security services and resources
sections.summary: AWS security capabilities and where to find security information (task 2.4).

items.name: Which security service?
items.summary: Threats → GuardDuty. Vulnerabilities → Inspector. PII in S3 → Macie. Investigation → Detective. Overview → Security Hub.
items.details: AWS security services each have a clear job: GuardDuty detects threats, Inspector finds software vulnerabilities, Macie finds sensitive data in S3, Detective investigates findings, Security Hub aggregates findings, Shield and WAF protect applications, and Firewall Manager applies rules across accounts.
items.example: A security team enables GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie and views their findings in Security Hub.

items.name: Third-party security products
items.summary: AWS Marketplace offers partner security tools such as firewalls, antivirus, and SIEM.
items.details: Customers can buy and deploy security products from AWS Partners through AWS Marketplace, with charges on their AWS bill.
items.example: A company deploys a partner next-generation firewall from AWS Marketplace.

items.name: Where to find security information
items.summary: AWS Security Center, AWS Security Blog, AWS Knowledge Center, and documentation.
items.details: AWS publishes security best practices, bulletins, and whitepapers through the AWS Security Center and the AWS Security Blog. The AWS Knowledge Center, part of AWS re:Post, answers common questions.
items.example: A team reads the AWS Security Blog for guidance on protecting a new workload.

items.name: Trusted Advisor security checks
items.summary: Flags issues such as open ports, no MFA on the root user, public S3 buckets, and exposed access keys.
items.details: Trusted Advisor’s security category helps identify common security issues across the account. Core security checks are available with Basic Support.
items.example: Trusted Advisor warns that a security group allows unrestricted SSH access.

sections.title: Deploying and operating in the AWS Cloud
sections.summary: Access methods and deployment models (task 3.1).

items.name: Deployment models: cloud, hybrid, on-premises
items.summary: Cloud: all in AWS. Hybrid: connect cloud and on-premises. On-premises: your own data center.
items.details: Cloud deployments run entirely in the cloud. Hybrid deployments connect cloud resources to on-premises infrastructure, for example with Direct Connect, VPN, Outposts, or Storage Gateway. On-premises (private cloud) deployments use virtualization in your own data center.
items.example: A bank keeps its core ledger on premises and runs its mobile app backend on AWS.
items.tip: Hybrid building blocks: Outposts, Storage Gateway, Direct Connect, and VPN.

items.name: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
items.summary: IaaS gives building blocks (EC2); PaaS manages the platform (Elastic Beanstalk); SaaS is finished software.
items.details: With IaaS you manage the operating system and everything above it. With PaaS the provider manages the infrastructure and runtime, and you manage the application. With SaaS you simply use the software.
items.example: Web-based email is SaaS; deploying code to Elastic Beanstalk is PaaS.

items.name: One-time operations vs repeatable processes
items.summary: Use the console for one-off tasks; automate anything you will do again.
items.details: Repeatable processes should be automated with the CLI, SDKs, or infrastructure as code so they are consistent, fast, and auditable.
items.example: A team templates its network design so every new account gets the same VPC layout.

sections.title: AWS global infrastructure
sections.summary: Regions, Availability Zones, and edge locations (task 3.2).

items.name: Regions
items.summary: Separate geographic areas, each with multiple Availability Zones; you choose where data lives.
items.details: Choose a Region based on compliance and data residency, proximity to users (latency), which services are available, and price.
items.example: A company picks the Sydney Region to serve Australian customers with low latency.
items.tip: Choosing a Region: compliance, latency, service availability, and cost.

items.name: Availability Zones
items.summary: One or more discrete data centers with redundant power and networking, isolated from other AZs.
items.details: AZs in a Region are physically separate and connected by low-latency links, so they don’t share single points of failure. Spreading an application across AZs gives high availability.
items.example: An application with instances in three AZs keeps running when one data center has a fire.
items.tip: Availability Zones don’t share single points of failure.

items.name: Edge locations
items.summary: Sites in many cities that serve CloudFront, Route 53, and Global Accelerator close to users.
items.details: Edge locations cache content and answer DNS queries near users, which reduces latency. There are many more edge locations than Regions.
items.example: A user in Lagos receives cached images from a nearby edge location.
items.tip: Edge locations don’t run your EC2 instances; they deliver content and DNS.

items.name: When to use multiple Regions
items.summary: Disaster recovery, business continuity, low latency for users worldwide, and data sovereignty.
items.details: Most applications get high availability from multiple AZs. Multiple Regions add protection against a Regional outage and serve users in other parts of the world, at extra cost and complexity.
items.example: A company replicates data to a second Region for disaster recovery.
items.tip: Survive an AZ failure → multi-AZ. Survive a Regional outage or serve another continent → multi-Region.

items.name: Local Zones and Outposts
items.summary: Local Zones put AWS infrastructure near large cities; Outposts brings AWS into your data center.
items.details: Local Zones extend a Region to metro areas for single-digit millisecond latency. Outposts runs AWS infrastructure on premises. (Wavelength, for 5G edge applications, is out of scope.)
items.example: A film studio renders video in a Local Zone close to its office.

sections.title: Choosing compute
sections.summary: EC2, containers, and serverless options (task 3.3).

items.name: EC2, containers, or serverless?
items.summary: EC2 for full control; ECS or EKS for containers; Lambda or Fargate when you don’t want to manage servers.
items.details: EC2 gives the most control and the most management. Containers package applications for portability; ECS and EKS orchestrate them. Lambda runs short event-driven functions, and Fargate runs containers without servers.
items.example: A team new to AWS runs its containerized API on Fargate to avoid managing servers.
items.tip: LEAST operational overhead → serverless (Lambda, Fargate).

items.name: Scaling up vs scaling out
items.summary: Scale up with a bigger instance, or out with more instances; scaling out also improves availability.
items.details: Vertical scaling changes the instance size and usually needs a restart. Horizontal scaling adds or removes instances behind a load balancer, which is what Auto Scaling does.
items.example: A web tier adds instances at peak times instead of running one very large server.
items.tip: Elasticity and high availability → horizontal scaling.

sections.title: Choosing a database
sections.summary: Relational, NoSQL, in-memory, and migration tools (task 3.4).

items.name: Purpose-built databases
items.summary: Relational (RDS, Aurora), key-value (DynamoDB), in-memory (ElastiCache), graph (Neptune), document (DocumentDB).
items.details: AWS offers a database for each data model, so you choose the one that matches your access pattern instead of forcing everything into one engine. Redshift is the data warehouse for analytics.
items.example: A shop keeps orders in Aurora, shopping carts in DynamoDB, and sessions in ElastiCache.

items.name: Transactions vs analytics
items.summary: Transactions for applications (RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB) vs analytics on large datasets (Redshift).
items.details: Online transaction processing (OLTP) handles many small reads and writes for an application. Online analytical processing (OLAP) runs complex queries over large amounts of historical data, which is what a data warehouse is for.
items.example: Orders are written to Aurora; last year’s sales trends are analyzed in Redshift.
items.tip: Reporting on years of data → Redshift, not the production database.

sections.title: Choosing storage
sections.summary: Object, block, file, and hybrid storage (task 3.6).

items.name: Object, block, and file storage
items.summary: Object: S3. Block: EBS and instance store. File: EFS and FSx. Hybrid caching: Storage Gateway.
items.details: Object storage keeps whole files with metadata, accessed over HTTPS. Block storage provides raw volumes attached to one instance. File storage provides shared file systems that many instances mount at once.
items.example: Images go to S3, a database’s disk is EBS, and a shared folder for many servers is EFS.

items.name: Backups and disaster recovery
items.summary: AWS Backup centralizes backups; Elastic Disaster Recovery fails servers over to AWS.
items.details: Use lifecycle rules for aging data, AWS Backup for scheduled backups and retention across services, and Elastic Disaster Recovery when servers must be running again in AWS within minutes.
items.example: A company keeps daily backups for 35 days with AWS Backup and protects critical servers with Elastic Disaster Recovery.

sections.title: AI/ML and analytics services
sections.summary: Which AI and analytics service does what (task 3.7).

items.name: AI services vs SageMaker AI
items.summary: Use pre-trained AI services for common tasks; use SageMaker AI to build custom models.
items.details: AI services such as Rekognition, Comprehend, and Transcribe solve common tasks through an API with no ML expertise. SageMaker AI is for teams that build, train, and deploy their own models. Amazon Q Developer is a generative AI assistant for building on AWS.
items.example: Detecting faces in photos → Rekognition; predicting churn from company data with a custom model → SageMaker AI.
items.tip: No ML expertise and a common task → a pre-trained AI service.

items.name: A typical analytics pipeline
items.summary: Ingest (Kinesis), store (S3), catalog and transform (Glue), query (Athena, Redshift), visualize (Quick Sight).
items.details: Streaming data arrives through Kinesis or Data Firehose, lands in S3, is cataloged and transformed with Glue, queried with Athena or Redshift, and presented in Quick Sight dashboards. EMR handles big data frameworks, and OpenSearch handles search and log analytics.
items.example: Clickstream data flows through Firehose to S3 and is analyzed with Athena and Quick Sight.

sections.title: Other service categories
sections.summary: Messaging, business applications, developer tools, end-user computing, web and mobile, and IoT (task 3.8).

items.name: Messages, alerts, and notifications
items.summary: Queue (SQS), push to many subscribers (SNS), route events (EventBridge), send email (SES).
items.details: Choose SQS to buffer and decouple work, SNS to push the same message to many subscribers or send alerts, EventBridge to route events between services and SaaS apps, and SES to send email to customers.
items.example: An order event goes to SNS, which fans out to SQS queues for shipping and billing.

items.name: Develop, deploy, and troubleshoot
items.summary: Build and test (CodeBuild), release (CodePipeline), trace (X-Ray), and script (CLI, SDKs).
items.details: CodeBuild compiles and tests code, CodePipeline automates releases, X-Ray traces requests to find bottlenecks, and the CLI and SDKs give programmatic access.
items.example: A release pipeline builds with CodeBuild, deploys automatically, and X-Ray shows which service slows down requests.

items.name: Virtual desktops and streamed apps
items.summary: WorkSpaces for full desktops, AppStream 2.0 for single apps, WorkSpaces Secure Browser for web apps.
items.details: These services present VMs or applications on end-user devices while the workload and data stay in AWS. WorkSpaces Secure Browser closes to new customers on 29 October 2026; AWS points new customers to WorkSpaces Applications (AppStream 2.0) with a Chrome image.
items.example: Call center staff use WorkSpaces desktops; designers stream one CAD application with AppStream 2.0.

items.name: Web, mobile, and IoT
items.summary: Amplify for building and hosting web and mobile apps; IoT Core to connect and manage devices.
items.details: Amplify helps front-end developers ship full-stack apps quickly. IoT Core securely connects devices and routes their data to other services.
items.example: A startup hosts its React app with Amplify and collects sensor data with IoT Core.

items.name: Business applications and support
items.summary: Amazon Connect for contact centers, Amazon SES for email, and AWS Support for help.
items.details: Amazon Connect runs a cloud contact center, SES sends email from applications, and AWS Support plans provide technical help.
items.example: A retailer opens a contact center with Amazon Connect and emails order updates with SES.

sections.title: Compute purchasing options
sections.summary: On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, Spot, and dedicated options (task 4.1).

items.name: On-Demand Instances
items.summary: Pay by the second or hour with no commitment; for short-term or unpredictable workloads.
items.details: On-Demand has the highest hourly price but complete flexibility. It suits new applications, spiky workloads, and anything that can’t be interrupted and runs for an unknown time.
items.example: A team tests a new application for two weeks on On-Demand Instances.
items.tip: Short-term, unpredictable, must not be interrupted → On-Demand.

items.name: Reserved Instances
items.summary: A 1- or 3-year commitment to an instance configuration for up to 72% off: Standard or Convertible.
items.details: Standard RIs give the biggest discount but allow few changes; Convertible RIs let you change the instance family, OS, or tenancy for a smaller discount. Paying more up front (All Upfront) gives a bigger discount than Partial or No Upfront.
items.example: A database that runs 24/7 for three years uses a 3-year Standard RI.
items.tip: Steady, predictable usage → Reserved Instances or Savings Plans.

items.name: Reserved Instance flexibility and sharing
items.summary: Regional RIs apply in any AZ and, for Linux, across sizes; discounts are shared across an organization.
items.details: A Regional RI’s discount applies to matching usage in any AZ of the Region and, for Linux instances with default tenancy, across sizes in the same family. With consolidated billing in AWS Organizations, unused RI discounts apply to matching usage in other accounts unless sharing is turned off.
items.example: An RI bought in one account covers a matching instance in another account in the same organization.
items.tip: RI discounts can be shared across accounts in an organization.

items.name: Savings Plans
items.summary: Commit to a dollar-per-hour spend for 1 or 3 years; Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate, and Lambda.
items.details: Savings Plans give lower prices in exchange for a commitment to a consistent amount of hourly spend. Compute Savings Plans are the most flexible (any instance family, size, Region, EC2, Fargate, and Lambda); EC2 Instance Savings Plans give bigger discounts for one instance family in one Region. SageMaker AI and Database Savings Plans also exist.
items.example: A company commits to $10 an hour of compute and saves on both EC2 and Lambda.
items.tip: Flexible commitment across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda → Compute Savings Plans.

items.name: Spot Instances
items.summary: Spare EC2 capacity at up to 90% off; AWS can reclaim it with a 2-minute warning.
items.details: Spot suits fault-tolerant, flexible workloads such as batch processing, CI builds, data analysis, and stateless web servers. It isn’t for workloads that can’t be interrupted.
items.example: A rendering farm processes thousands of frames on Spot Instances overnight.
items.tip: Interruptible, flexible workloads at the lowest price → Spot.

items.name: Dedicated Hosts vs Dedicated Instances
items.summary: Both use single-tenant hardware; Dedicated Hosts also show physical cores and sockets for licensing.
items.details: Dedicated Instances run on hardware dedicated to one customer. Dedicated Hosts give you a whole physical server, control over instance placement, and visibility of physical cores and sockets, which some software licenses and compliance rules require.
items.example: A company uses Dedicated Hosts to bring Windows Server licenses counted per physical core.
items.tip: Per-core or per-socket licenses (BYOL) or server-bound compliance → Dedicated Hosts.

items.name: On-Demand Capacity Reservations
items.summary: Reserve EC2 capacity in a specific AZ for any duration, with no long-term commitment.
items.details: Capacity Reservations guarantee capacity will be there when you need it, for example for a big event or disaster recovery. You pay the On-Demand rate whether or not you use it; Savings Plans or Regional RIs can reduce the price.
items.example: A retailer reserves capacity in one AZ for Black Friday.
items.tip: Guarantee capacity in a specific AZ → Capacity Reservations.

sections.title: Data transfer and storage pricing
sections.summary: Inbound and outbound transfer and storage tiers (task 4.1).

items.name: Data transfer costs
items.summary: Inbound from the internet is free; outbound to the internet and between Regions is charged.
items.details: Data transferred into AWS from the internet is free. Data transferred out to the internet is charged per GB, with lower rates at higher volumes. Transfer between Regions is charged, and transfer between AZs in the same Region usually is too.
items.example: Serving videos through CloudFront can cost less than serving them directly from EC2.
items.tip: Inbound → free. Outbound and inter-Region → charged.

items.name: Storage pricing
items.summary: S3 charges for storage by class, requests, retrievals for some classes, and data transfer out.
items.details: Cheaper S3 storage classes have retrieval fees and minimum storage durations. EBS is charged for the provisioned size, whether or not the space is used.
items.example: An archive that is rarely read costs less in Glacier, but frequent retrievals would cancel the savings.
items.tip: EBS: pay for provisioned GB. S3: pay for what you store.

items.name: AWS Free Tier
items.summary: New accounts get credits; more than 30 services also have always-free monthly allowances.
items.details: Since July 2025, new accounts receive $100 in credits and can earn up to $100 more, on either a free plan (up to 6 months) or a paid plan. Some services also have always-free usage or short free trials.
items.example: A student explores AWS on the free plan using credits.
items.tip: Always-free offers, credits, and free trials are different kinds of free usage.

sections.title: Billing, budgets, and cost management
sections.summary: Tools to estimate, track, alert on, and allocate costs (task 4.2).

items.name: Which cost tool?
items.summary: Estimate (Pricing Calculator), alert (Budgets), analyze (Cost Explorer), detailed data (Cost and Usage Reports).
items.details: Use the Pricing Calculator before you build, AWS Budgets to get alerts on spend, Cost Explorer to analyze and forecast costs, and Cost and Usage Reports for the most detailed line-item data.
items.example: A team estimates a project with the Pricing Calculator, then sets a budget alert once it is live.
items.tip: Estimate before deploying → Pricing Calculator.

items.name: AWS Pricing Calculator
items.summary: Estimate the monthly cost of an architecture before you build it.
items.details: The Pricing Calculator lets you model services and configurations, compare options, and share or export estimates.
items.example: An architect estimates the cost of a three-tier web app before the project is approved.

items.name: Cost allocation tags
items.summary: Tag resources and activate the tags in Billing to see costs by project, team, or environment.
items.details: AWS-generated tags and user-defined tags must be activated before they appear in Cost Explorer and Cost and Usage Reports.
items.example: Costs are split by a CostCenter tag so each department can be charged.
items.tip: Allocate costs to departments or projects → cost allocation tags.

items.name: Consolidated billing in AWS Organizations
items.summary: One payer account, combined volume discounts, and shared RI and Savings Plans discounts.
items.details: The management account receives one bill for all member accounts. Usage is aggregated for volume pricing tiers, and RI and Savings Plans discounts can be shared.
items.example: A company with 12 accounts receives one bill and reaches cheaper S3 pricing tiers sooner.

sections.title: Technical resources and AWS Support
sections.summary: Documentation, support plans, partners, and help (task 4.3).

items.name: Where to find help
items.summary: Documentation, whitepapers, AWS re:Post, AWS Knowledge Center, AWS Prescriptive Guidance, and the Architecture Center.
items.details: Documentation and whitepapers explain services and best practices; re:Post is the community Q&A site; the Knowledge Center answers common questions; Prescriptive Guidance gives proven strategies and patterns; the Architecture Center offers reference architectures.
items.example: A developer finds the fix for a common error in the AWS Knowledge Center.

items.name: Choosing a support plan
items.summary: Basic (free), Business Support+ (24/7 experts), Enterprise (designated TAM), Unified Operations (fastest response).
items.details: Match the plan to the need: Basic for account and billing help only; Business Support+ for 24/7 technical support and all Trusted Advisor checks; Enterprise for a designated TAM and proactive guidance; Unified Operations for mission-critical workloads that need a 5-minute response.
items.example: A company that needs a designated technical account manager chooses Enterprise Support.
items.tip: Designated TAM → Enterprise or Unified Operations.

items.name: AWS Support Center
items.summary: Open and manage support cases; account and billing cases are available to every customer.
items.details: Support cases are opened in the Support Center. All customers can open account and billing cases; technical cases need a paid plan.
items.example: A customer opens a billing case about an unexpected charge.

items.name: AWS Trust & Safety
items.summary: Report suspected abuse of AWS resources, such as spam, phishing, or attacks from AWS IP addresses.
items.details: If AWS resources are used for illegal or abusive activity, anyone can report it to the AWS Trust & Safety team through the abuse reporting process described in the Acceptable Use Policy.
items.example: A company receiving phishing emails from an AWS-hosted server reports it to AWS Trust & Safety.
items.tip: Report abuse → AWS Trust & Safety, not AWS Support.

items.name: AWS Partner Network (APN)
items.summary: Consulting partners and system integrators, plus technology partners (ISVs) whose software runs on AWS.
items.details: AWS Partners include system integrators (SIs) and consulting firms that help customers design, build, and migrate, and independent software vendors (ISVs) that sell products, often through AWS Marketplace. Partners benefit from training and certification, events, and volume discounts.
items.example: A company hires an AWS Partner to migrate its data center.
items.tip: Hands-on help to build or migrate → an AWS Partner or AWS Professional Services.

items.name: AWS Professional Services and solutions architects
items.summary: AWS experts who help with large projects, migrations, and architecture.
items.details: AWS Professional Services works with customers’ teams, often alongside partners, to deliver outcomes. AWS solutions architects give architectural guidance to customers.
items.example: A bank engages AWS Professional Services to plan a regulated migration.

items.name: AWS Health and Trusted Advisor for operations
items.summary: Track AWS events that affect you, and act on cost and resilience recommendations.
items.details: The AWS Health Dashboard and AWS Health API report events that affect your resources, and Trusted Advisor highlights cost optimization opportunities such as idle resources.
items.example: An operations team automates responses to scheduled maintenance events with the AWS Health API.

sections.title: Exam format & scoring
sections.summary: What to expect on exam day and how CLF-C02 is scored.

items.name: 65 questions in 90 minutes
items.summary: 50 scored and 15 unscored questions; you can’t tell which ones are unscored.
items.details: The exam has 65 questions. Fifteen are unscored questions that AWS is trying out, and they look like the rest. You have 90 minutes, about 80 seconds per question.
items.example: Aim to finish a first pass in about 60 minutes, leaving 30 minutes for flagged questions.
items.tip: Treat every question as scored, but don’t sink time into one odd question.

items.name: Scaled score and compensatory scoring
items.summary: Scores run from 100 to 1,000 and 700 passes; you don’t need to pass each domain.
items.details: Results are a scaled score. The compensatory model means strong domains can make up for weaker ones; only the overall score decides pass or fail.
items.example: Strong results in Domain 3 (34%) can offset a weaker Domain 4 (12%).
items.tip: Split study time by weight: 24% / 30% / 34% / 12%.

items.name: Two question types
items.summary: Multiple choice (1 of 4) and multiple response (2 or more of 5 or more). No ordering or matching.
items.details: Unlike some newer AWS exams, CLF-C02 has only multiple choice and multiple response questions. Multiple response questions say how many answers to select, and there is no partial credit.
items.example: “Which TWO actions…? (Select TWO.)” needs both correct answers to score.
items.tip: One wrong selection in a multiple response question makes it wrong.

items.name: No penalty for guessing
items.summary: Blank answers score the same as wrong ones, so answer every question.
items.details: Unanswered questions are marked incorrect. Always pick an answer, even for a question you plan to revisit.
items.example: With two minutes left, guess the remaining questions rather than leaving them blank.

items.name: Booking, cost, and validity
items.summary: $100 USD, at a Pearson VUE center or online with a proctor; valid for 3 years.
items.details: You can test at a Pearson VUE center or online. There are no prerequisites, and the certification is valid for three years. Non-native English speakers can request the ESL +30 accommodation before booking.
items.example: If you test online, run the system check in advance and clear your desk.

sections.title: Qualifier keywords
sections.summary: Words in the question that decide between otherwise valid answers.

items.name: LEAST operational overhead / effort
items.summary: Choose the most managed or serverless option that meets the need.
items.details: Managed services (RDS, DynamoDB, Lambda, Fargate, Elastic Beanstalk) beat running the same thing yourself on EC2 when the question asks for the least management.
items.example: A relational database with the least administration → Amazon RDS, not a database installed on EC2.
items.tip: Options that mention managing EC2 instances are usually wrong for this qualifier.

items.name: MOST cost-effective
items.summary: The cheapest option that still meets every stated requirement.
items.details: Match the pricing model to the workload: Spot for interruptible work, Savings Plans or RIs for steady use, On-Demand for short or unpredictable use, and cheaper storage classes for rarely accessed data.
items.example: A nightly batch job that can restart if interrupted → Spot Instances.
items.tip: The cheapest option is wrong if it breaks a requirement such as “can’t be interrupted”.

items.name: Highly available / fault tolerant
items.summary: Look for multiple Availability Zones, load balancing, and managed replication.
items.details: High availability comes from removing single points of failure: multiple AZs, Elastic Load Balancing, Auto Scaling, RDS Multi-AZ, and services that replicate automatically.
items.example: Make a web app highly available → instances in at least two AZs behind a load balancer.
items.tip: Multi-Region is for disaster recovery or global users, not the default answer for availability.

items.name: Customer vs AWS responsibility
items.summary: Decide whether the task is “of the cloud” (AWS) or “in the cloud” (customer).
items.details: Shared responsibility questions often hide the answer in the service type: on EC2 the customer patches the OS, on RDS and Lambda AWS does. Data, IAM, and configuration are always the customer’s.
items.example: Who encrypts customer data in S3? The customer chooses and configures the encryption.

items.name: Hidden constraints
items.summary: Phrases like “no upfront commitment”, “minimal downtime”, or “data must stay in the country” rule options out.
items.details: Find the one requirement that eliminates otherwise valid answers before reading the options.
items.example: “Without long-term commitment” rules out Reserved Instances and Savings Plans.
items.tip: Don’t add requirements that the question doesn’t state.

sections.title: Answering technique
sections.summary: How to work through CLF questions efficiently.

items.name: Read the question sentence first
items.summary: Find out what is asked before reading the scenario details.
items.details: The last sentence tells you whether you are choosing a service, a pricing model, a support plan, or a responsibility. Then read the scenario for the constraint that matters.
items.example: If the question ends “Which AWS service…?”, look for the task keyword: monitor, audit, encrypt, cache, queue.

items.name: Eliminate, then compare
items.summary: Remove options that solve a different problem, then compare the rest on the key requirement.
items.details: Distractors are real AWS services from the same family. Knowing the one-line purpose of each service lets you eliminate quickly.
items.example: CloudTrail, Config, and CloudWatch all relate to monitoring, but only CloudTrail answers “who made this API call?”.

items.name: Multiple response questions
items.summary: Judge each option on its own and select exactly the number asked.
items.details: Evaluate every option as true or false against the scenario. Don’t pick an option you can’t justify.
items.example: “Which TWO are customer responsibilities?” → check each option against the shared responsibility model.

items.name: Pacing and flagging
items.summary: About 80 seconds per question; flag and move on rather than getting stuck.
items.details: Answer every question on the first pass, flagging uncertain ones, and revisit flagged questions with the remaining time.
items.example: At question 33 you should have about 45 minutes left.
items.tip: Change an answer only when you find a specific reason.

sections.title: Common traps
sections.summary: Patterns in AWS’s own practice questions that catch fast readers.

items.name: Look-alike names
items.summary: Amazon Connect isn’t Direct Connect, DAX isn’t Global Accelerator, and Client VPN isn’t Site-to-Site VPN.
items.details: AWS reuses words across unrelated services. Amazon Connect is a contact center; AWS Direct Connect is a network link. DAX caches DynamoDB reads; Global Accelerator speeds up network paths. Client VPN connects people; Site-to-Site VPN connects networks. Polly speaks text, Transcribe writes down speech, Translate changes the language, and Textract reads documents.
items.example: A data center needs a private link to AWS → Direct Connect, even when “Amazon Connect” is also an option.
items.tip: Match the service’s job, not a word in its name.

items.name: Check the scope: AZ, Region, or global
items.summary: Multi-AZ adds availability, not lower latency for distant users, and a load balancer stays in one Region.
items.details: Availability Zones are inside one Region, so spreading across them protects against a data center failure but doesn’t bring an app closer to users on other continents. Elastic Load Balancing spreads traffic across AZs in one Region. For distant users, use more Regions and CloudFront; to route between Regions, use Route 53 or Global Accelerator.
items.example: Users in Asia see slow responses from an app in two AZs in Europe → deploy in an Asian Region and use CloudFront, not a third AZ.
items.tip: IAM, Route 53, and CloudFront are global; EC2, Elastic Load Balancing, and RDS are Regional.

items.name: Options that do part of the job
items.summary: DMS moves database data, not the server it runs on, and Route 53 can’t speed up a single origin.
items.details: Some wrong options are real services that cover part of the requirement. DMS migrates data between databases, while AWS MGN moves whole servers with their apps and databases. Cost and Usage Reports show costs but don’t combine bills; AWS Organizations does. Route 53 latency routing needs several endpoints to choose between.
items.example: Move a Linux server that runs an app and its database to EC2 as is → AWS MGN.
items.tip: Check that the option meets every part of the requirement, not just one.

items.name: Plain wording that points to a service
items.summary: “Existing internet connection” and “encrypted” → Site-to-Site VPN; “consistent and private” → Direct Connect.
items.details: AWS practice questions often describe the need instead of naming the feature. “Encryption in transit” → TLS certificates from ACM. “Relational” → RDS or Aurora, not DynamoDB. “Programmatic access” → an access key ID plus a secret access key. “Unused EC2 capacity” → Spot Instances. “Read text aloud” → Polly.
items.example: Alert the whole development team when a test fails → Amazon SNS.

items.name: Older support plan names
items.summary: AWS’s practice questions still use Developer, Business, and Enterprise; answer them with the older rules.
items.details: The exam guide now lists Basic, Business Support+, Enterprise, and Unified Operations, but the official practice set (checked October 2026) still asks about the older plans. Under those, Developer had business-hours email support, Business was the minimum for 24/7 phone and chat and all Trusted Advisor checks, Enterprise On-Ramp added a pool of TAMs, and Enterprise had a designated TAM.
items.example: The minimum older plan with phone support → Business Support.
items.tip: Use whichever set of names the options use.

items.name: Fast answers are where traps work
items.summary: You have about 80 seconds per question; spend some of it checking scope and wording.
items.details: Most of these traps are easy to spot once you read the requirement word by word. In multiple response questions, judge each option as true or false on its own before choosing two.
items.example: Before selecting, ask: does this option meet every requirement, at the right scope, with the right service?

sections.title: Services that changed recently
sections.summary: In-scope services that AWS closed to new customers or renamed, and how to answer about them.

items.name: WorkSpaces Secure Browser (29 October 2026)
items.summary: New customers can’t sign up from 29 October 2026; existing customers keep it. The exam guide still lists it.
items.details: AWS recommends WorkSpaces Applications (formerly AppStream 2.0) with a Chrome image for new browser-isolation setups. On the exam, browser-only secure access to internal web apps still points to Secure Browser.
items.example: Contractors on personal laptops need an internal web portal with downloads blocked → WorkSpaces Secure Browser.

items.name: Migration Hub and Application Discovery Service (November 2025)
items.summary: Both closed to new customers on 7 November 2025; AWS Transform now covers discovery and tracking.
items.details: Existing customers keep using them, and the exam guide still lists both, so answer with them when a scenario asks to discover servers or track migrations. Application Migration Service, DMS, and Migration Evaluator are unaffected.
items.example: Track the progress of migrations across several tools → Migration Hub.

items.name: Amazon Q Business (30 July 2026)
items.summary: Closed to new customers; Amazon Quick is its successor. Amazon Q Developer is unaffected.
items.details: The exam guide lists Amazon Q. An assistant that answers employees from company documents was Amazon Q Business; for new setups AWS points to Amazon Quick. An assistant that writes and explains code is Amazon Q Developer.
items.example: Help developers upgrade old code in the IDE → Amazon Q Developer.

items.name: Same services, new names
items.summary: AppStream 2.0 is now WorkSpaces Applications, QuickSight is Quick Sight, and Kinesis Data Firehose is Data Firehose.
items.details: Questions may use either name. The vault-based Amazon Glacier service closed to new customers in November 2025, but the S3 Glacier storage classes that exam questions ask about are unaffected.
items.example: Stream one desktop application to a browser → AppStream 2.0 (WorkSpaces Applications).

sections.title: Trigger phrases → answers
sections.summary: Common question wording and the service or concept it points to.

items.name: “Who made this API call?”
items.summary: → AWS CloudTrail.
items.details: CloudTrail records API activity with the identity, time, and source.
items.example: An auditor finds who terminated an instance.

items.name: “How was this resource configured last month?” / “Is it compliant?”
items.summary: → AWS Config.
items.details: Config keeps configuration history and evaluates rules.
items.example: A team checks that all buckets block public access.

items.name: “Monitor CPU and alert when it’s high”
items.summary: → Amazon CloudWatch (alarm) + SNS.
items.details: CloudWatch collects metrics and triggers alarms that can notify through SNS.
items.example: An alarm emails the team when CPU stays above 80%.

items.name: “Detect malicious activity or compromised credentials”
items.summary: → Amazon GuardDuty.
items.details: GuardDuty analyzes logs with threat intelligence and ML.
items.example: Unusual API calls from a foreign IP are flagged.

items.name: “Scan instances or containers for vulnerabilities”
items.summary: → Amazon Inspector.
items.details: Inspector finds known software vulnerabilities and network exposure.
items.example: An outdated package on EC2 is reported.

items.name: “Find PII in S3”
items.summary: → Amazon Macie.
items.details: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 buckets.
items.example: Credit card numbers are found in a log bucket.

items.name: “DDoS protection” vs “SQL injection”
items.summary: → AWS Shield vs AWS WAF.
items.details: Shield protects against DDoS attacks; WAF filters malicious web requests.
items.example: A website blocks SQL injection with WAF and relies on Shield Standard for DDoS.

items.name: “Download AWS compliance reports”
items.summary: → AWS Artifact.
items.details: Artifact provides SOC, ISO, and PCI reports and agreements.
items.example: An auditor downloads AWS’s SOC 2 report.

items.name: “Lift and shift servers”
items.summary: → Rehost with AWS Application Migration Service.
items.details: Rehosting moves servers without changing them.
items.example: VMware VMs are replicated to EC2.

items.name: “Migrate a database with minimal downtime”
items.summary: → AWS DMS (plus SCT when engines differ).
items.details: DMS replicates data while the source stays online.
items.example: Oracle moves to Aurora PostgreSQL.

items.name: “Low latency for global users” / “cache content”
items.summary: → Amazon CloudFront.
items.details: CloudFront caches content at edge locations.
items.example: Images load faster for users in Asia.

items.name: “Dedicated private connection with consistent performance”
items.summary: → AWS Direct Connect.
items.details: Direct Connect is a dedicated line that doesn’t use the internet.
items.example: A bank links its data center to AWS.

items.name: “NoSQL, key-value, millisecond latency at any scale”
items.summary: → Amazon DynamoDB.
items.details: DynamoDB is a serverless NoSQL database.
items.example: A game stores player sessions.

items.name: “Data warehouse” vs “SQL on files in S3”
items.summary: → Amazon Redshift vs Amazon Athena.
items.details: Redshift is a data warehouse; Athena queries S3 directly without servers.
items.example: Analysts query logs in S3 with Athena.

items.name: “Decouple components” vs “notify many subscribers”
items.summary: → Amazon SQS vs Amazon SNS.
items.details: SQS queues messages for consumers; SNS pushes messages to many subscribers.
items.example: Orders queue in SQS; alerts go out through SNS.

items.name: “Interruptible workload at the lowest cost”
items.summary: → Spot Instances.
items.details: Spot uses spare capacity at up to 90% off and can be reclaimed.
items.example: Batch rendering runs overnight.

items.name: “Steady usage for 1 or 3 years”
items.summary: → Savings Plans or Reserved Instances.
items.details: Commitments give large discounts for predictable usage.
items.example: A 24/7 database uses a 3-year commitment.

items.name: “Estimate costs before deploying”
items.summary: → AWS Pricing Calculator.
items.details: The Pricing Calculator models the cost of an architecture.
items.example: An architect prices a new project.

items.name: “Alert when spending exceeds a threshold”
items.summary: → AWS Budgets.
items.details: Budgets sends alerts on actual or forecasted spend.
items.example: An email arrives at 80% of the monthly budget.

items.name: “Designated technical account manager”
items.summary: → Enterprise Support (or Unified Operations).
items.details: A designated TAM comes with Enterprise Support and above.
items.example: A bank wants a named TAM.

items.name: “Provision infrastructure as code” / “repeatable environments”
items.summary: → AWS CloudFormation.
items.details: CloudFormation deploys resources from templates.
items.example: Three identical environments are created from one template.

items.name: “Deploy a web app without managing infrastructure”
items.summary: → AWS Elastic Beanstalk.
items.details: Beanstalk provisions and manages the environment for your code.
items.example: A developer uploads a Java app.

items.name: “Employees sign in once to many AWS accounts”
items.summary: → AWS IAM Identity Center.
items.details: Identity Center provides workforce single sign-on.
items.example: Staff use corporate credentials to reach each account.

items.name: “Sign-up and sign-in for app users”
items.summary: → Amazon Cognito.
items.details: Cognito manages customer identities for apps.
items.example: Shoppers sign in with Google.

sections.title: Security services
sections.summary: Security services that sound alike but do different jobs.

items.name: Security groups vs network ACLs
items.summary: Security group: stateful, instance level, allow only. Network ACL: stateless, subnet level, allow and deny.
items.details: Security groups allow traffic to instances and automatically allow the return traffic. Network ACLs filter traffic at the subnet boundary, evaluate numbered rules in order, can explicitly deny, and need rules in both directions.
items.example: Deny traffic from one malicious IP range for a whole subnet → network ACL.
items.tip: Only network ACLs can deny traffic.

items.name: Shield vs WAF vs Firewall Manager
items.summary: Shield stops DDoS; WAF filters web requests; Firewall Manager applies these rules across accounts.
items.details: AWS Shield protects against DDoS attacks (Standard is automatic and free; Advanced is paid). AWS WAF blocks web exploits such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. AWS Firewall Manager centrally manages WAF, Shield Advanced, and security group rules across an organization.
items.example: A company uses WAF on its load balancers, and Firewall Manager to apply the same rules in every account.
items.tip: Layer 7 web attacks → WAF. Volumetric DDoS → Shield.

items.name: GuardDuty vs Inspector vs Macie vs Detective vs Security Hub
items.summary: Threats; vulnerabilities; PII in S3; investigation; one dashboard for everything.
items.details: GuardDuty detects malicious activity from logs. Inspector scans EC2, container images, and Lambda for software vulnerabilities. Macie finds sensitive data in S3. Detective helps investigate the root cause of findings. Security Hub aggregates findings and runs compliance checks.
items.example: GuardDuty flags an attack, Detective shows how it unfolded, and Security Hub displays it with other findings.

items.name: KMS vs CloudHSM vs ACM vs Secrets Manager
items.summary: Managed keys; dedicated HSMs; TLS certificates; rotating secrets.
items.details: KMS manages encryption keys used by AWS services. CloudHSM provides single-tenant hardware security modules under your control. ACM issues and renews SSL/TLS certificates. Secrets Manager stores and rotates secrets such as database passwords.
items.example: An app uses KMS to encrypt data, ACM for HTTPS, and Secrets Manager for its database password.
items.tip: Rotate a database password automatically → Secrets Manager.

items.name: IAM vs IAM Identity Center vs Cognito vs Directory Service
items.summary: Account permissions; workforce SSO; app users; Microsoft Active Directory.
items.details: IAM defines users, roles, and permissions in an account. IAM Identity Center gives employees single sign-on to many accounts. Cognito manages the users of your web and mobile apps. Directory Service runs or connects to Microsoft Active Directory.
items.example: Employees use Identity Center; customers of the app sign in with Cognito.

sections.title: Monitoring, governance & accounts
sections.summary: Logging, recommendations, and multi-account services.

items.name: CloudTrail vs Config vs CloudWatch
items.summary: Who did what; how resources are configured; how resources perform.
items.details: CloudTrail records API calls and account activity. Config records configuration history and checks compliance with rules. CloudWatch collects metrics and logs and triggers alarms.
items.example: Who opened port 22? → CloudTrail. Is port 22 open now and since when? → Config. Is the server overloaded? → CloudWatch.

items.name: Trusted Advisor vs Health Dashboard vs Compute Optimizer vs Well-Architected Tool
items.summary: Account checks; AWS events affecting you; rightsizing; workload review.
items.details: Trusted Advisor runs automated best-practice checks across the account. The AWS Health Dashboard shows AWS events affecting your resources. Compute Optimizer recommends resource sizes. The Well-Architected Tool guides a question-based review of one workload.
items.example: Idle load balancers flagged → Trusted Advisor. Scheduled maintenance on your instance → Health Dashboard.

items.name: Organizations vs Control Tower vs Service Catalog vs RAM
items.summary: Manage accounts and SCPs; set up a governed landing zone; approved products; share resources.
items.details: Organizations groups accounts, applies SCPs, and consolidates billing. Control Tower automates a best-practice multi-account setup on top of Organizations. Service Catalog offers approved products for self-service. RAM shares resources such as subnets across accounts.
items.example: Quickly set up a governed multi-account environment → Control Tower.

sections.title: Compute & storage
sections.summary: Compute and storage options with overlapping uses.

items.name: EC2 vs Lambda vs Fargate vs Elastic Beanstalk vs Lightsail vs Batch
items.summary: Full control; event-driven functions; serverless containers; PaaS; simple VPS; batch jobs.
items.details: EC2 gives full control of virtual servers. Lambda runs code on events, up to 15 minutes per run. Fargate runs containers without servers. Elastic Beanstalk deploys apps and manages the environment. Lightsail offers simple, fixed-price servers. Batch runs large numbers of batch jobs.
items.example: Resize images whenever they’re uploaded → Lambda.

items.name: ECS vs EKS vs Fargate vs ECR
items.summary: AWS-native orchestration; Kubernetes; serverless compute for both; image registry.
items.details: ECS and EKS orchestrate containers, EKS using Kubernetes. Either can run containers on EC2 or on Fargate, which removes server management. ECR stores the container images.
items.example: A team that already uses Kubernetes → EKS.

items.name: S3 vs EBS vs instance store vs EFS vs FSx
items.summary: Objects; block volume for one instance; temporary disk; shared Linux files; managed file systems such as Windows.
