items.details: S3 stores objects accessed over HTTPS. EBS is persistent block storage attached to one instance in one AZ. Instance store is fast but temporary. EFS is a shared NFS file system for Linux. FSx provides managed file systems such as Windows File Server.
items.example: Many Linux instances need the same files → EFS.

items.name: S3 storage classes
items.summary: Standard; Intelligent-Tiering; Standard-IA; One Zone-IA; Glacier Instant, Flexible, and Deep Archive.
items.details: Choose by access pattern and retrieval time: frequent access → Standard; unknown pattern → Intelligent-Tiering; infrequent but immediate → Standard-IA (or One Zone-IA if data can be recreated); archive with millisecond access → Glacier Instant Retrieval; archive with minutes to hours → Glacier Flexible Retrieval; cheapest, rarely accessed → Glacier Deep Archive.
items.example: Re-creatable thumbnails accessed rarely → S3 One Zone-IA.
items.tip: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, so it suits only data you can recreate.

items.name: AWS Backup vs Elastic Disaster Recovery vs Storage Gateway
items.summary: Scheduled backups; fast server failover; hybrid access to cloud storage.
items.details: AWS Backup schedules and retains backups across services. Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates servers so they can be launched in AWS within minutes. Storage Gateway gives on-premises apps access to cloud storage with a local cache.
items.example: Keep 35 days of database backups → AWS Backup.

items.name: CloudFormation vs Elastic Beanstalk
items.summary: Define any infrastructure as code vs deploy an application and let AWS manage the environment.
items.details: CloudFormation provisions any set of AWS resources from templates. Elastic Beanstalk focuses on deploying application code and manages the instances, load balancer, and scaling for you (it uses CloudFormation behind the scenes).
items.example: Developers who just want to upload code → Elastic Beanstalk.

sections.title: Databases & analytics
sections.summary: Databases and analytics services for different data needs.

items.name: RDS vs Aurora vs DynamoDB vs ElastiCache vs Neptune vs DocumentDB vs Redshift
items.summary: Relational; high-performance relational; NoSQL; cache; graph; MongoDB-compatible; data warehouse.
items.details: RDS runs common relational engines. Aurora is AWS’s MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible engine with higher performance. DynamoDB is serverless NoSQL. ElastiCache is an in-memory cache. Neptune stores graphs. DocumentDB is MongoDB-compatible. Redshift is the data warehouse.
items.example: Social network relationships → Neptune.

items.name: Athena vs Redshift vs EMR vs Glue vs Kinesis vs Quick Sight vs OpenSearch
items.summary: SQL on S3; warehouse; big data frameworks; ETL; streaming; dashboards; search and logs.
items.details: Athena queries S3 with SQL. Redshift is a data warehouse. EMR runs Spark and Hadoop. Glue is serverless ETL with a data catalog. Kinesis ingests streaming data. Quick Sight builds dashboards. OpenSearch Service powers search and log analytics.
items.example: Real-time clickstream ingestion → Kinesis; weekly executive dashboard → Quick Sight.

sections.title: Networking
sections.summary: Connectivity and content delivery options.

items.name: Site-to-Site VPN vs Direct Connect vs Client VPN
items.summary: Encrypted over the internet; dedicated private line; individual remote users.
items.details: Site-to-Site VPN is fast to set up and cheap but depends on the internet. Direct Connect is a dedicated connection with consistent performance that takes weeks to set up. Client VPN connects individual users.
items.example: Connect a data center by tomorrow → Site-to-Site VPN.

items.name: VPC peering vs Transit Gateway vs PrivateLink
items.summary: Connect two VPCs; hub for many networks; private access to services.
items.details: VPC peering connects two VPCs directly and isn’t transitive. Transit Gateway is a central hub for many VPCs and on-premises networks. PrivateLink exposes a service privately through interface endpoints.
items.example: Connect 50 VPCs and two offices → Transit Gateway.

items.name: CloudFront vs Global Accelerator vs Route 53
items.summary: Cache content at the edge; static IPs and fast failover for TCP/UDP; DNS and routing policies.
items.details: CloudFront caches and delivers content near users. Global Accelerator routes traffic over the AWS network to healthy endpoints through two static IP addresses. Route 53 resolves domain names and routes by latency, location, weight, or health.
items.example: Fail over between Regions at the DNS level → Route 53.

items.name: Internet gateway vs NAT gateway
items.summary: Two-way internet access for public subnets vs outbound-only access for private subnets.
items.details: An internet gateway lets resources with public IPs communicate with the internet. A NAT gateway lets instances in private subnets start outbound connections without being reachable from the internet.
items.example: Private servers download patches → NAT gateway.

sections.title: Migration, messaging & end-user computing
sections.summary: Migration tools, integration services, and desktops.

items.name: The six migration services
items.summary: Discover servers; build a business case; track progress; move servers (MGN); move data (DMS); convert schemas (SCT).
items.details: Application Discovery Service inventories on-premises servers. Migration Evaluator builds a cost business case. Migration Hub tracks progress. Application Migration Service rehosts servers. DMS migrates database data. SCT converts schemas between engines.
items.example: Oracle to PostgreSQL → SCT converts the schema, DMS moves the data.

items.name: SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge vs Step Functions vs SES
items.summary: Queue; push to many; route events; orchestrate steps; send email.
items.details: SQS buffers messages for consumers to pull. SNS pushes messages to many subscribers. EventBridge routes events from AWS services and SaaS apps by rules. Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows. SES sends email to customers.
items.example: Run a five-step order workflow with retries → Step Functions.

items.name: WorkSpaces vs AppStream 2.0 vs WorkSpaces Secure Browser
items.summary: Full virtual desktop; stream one application; secure access to web apps.
items.details: WorkSpaces provides persistent virtual desktops. AppStream 2.0 (now WorkSpaces Applications) streams individual desktop applications. WorkSpaces Secure Browser streams a browser for internal web apps.
items.example: Give designers one CAD application in the browser → AppStream 2.0.
items.tip: Secure Browser closes to new customers on 29 October 2026, but the exam guide still lists it for browser-only access.

sections.title: Pricing & support
sections.summary: Purchasing options, cost tools, and support plans.

items.name: On-Demand vs Reserved vs Savings Plans vs Spot vs Dedicated Hosts
items.summary: Flexible; committed configuration; committed spend; interruptible; physical server.
items.details: On-Demand: no commitment, highest price. Reserved Instances: 1 or 3 years for an instance configuration. Savings Plans: 1 or 3 years of committed hourly spend, more flexible. Spot: up to 90% off, can be interrupted. Dedicated Hosts: a physical server for licensing or compliance.
items.example: Unknown workload for a two-week project → On-Demand.
items.tip: Capacity Reservations guarantee capacity in an AZ but give no discount by themselves.

items.name: Pricing Calculator vs Budgets vs Cost Explorer vs Cost and Usage Reports
items.summary: Estimate before; alert during; analyze after; most detailed data.
items.details: The Pricing Calculator estimates costs before you build. Budgets alerts when spend crosses thresholds. Cost Explorer visualizes and forecasts costs. Cost and Usage Reports give line-item data for custom analysis.
items.example: See which service caused last month’s cost increase → Cost Explorer.

items.name: Basic vs Business Support+ vs Enterprise vs Unified Operations
items.summary: Free; 24/7 experts and full Trusted Advisor; designated TAM; fastest response.
items.details: Basic: account and billing help and core Trusted Advisor checks. Business Support+ (from $29/month): 24/7 technical support, AI-assisted help, all checks. Enterprise (from $5,000/month): designated TAM, 15-minute critical response. Unified Operations (from $50,000/month): 5-minute response and incident management engineers.
items.example: Cheapest plan with all Trusted Advisor checks → Business Support+.
items.tip: If the options use the older names (Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp), use the older rules: 24/7 phone and chat started at Business.

sections.title: Cloud concepts
sections.summary: Terms that are easy to mix up in Domains 1 and 3.

items.name: Regions vs Availability Zones vs edge locations vs Local Zones vs Outposts
items.summary: Geographic area; isolated data centers; content delivery sites; metro extensions; AWS on premises.
items.details: A Region contains multiple AZs. AZs are isolated data centers within a Region. Edge locations deliver CloudFront and Route 53 close to users. Local Zones extend a Region to a city. Outposts puts AWS hardware in your data center.
items.example: Run AWS services in your own building → Outposts.

items.name: Elasticity vs scalability vs high availability vs fault tolerance vs agility
items.summary: Auto-adjust to demand; grow capacity; minimal downtime; no interruption; speed of change.
items.details: Elasticity grows and shrinks automatically with demand. Scalability is the ability to handle growth. High availability minimizes downtime. Fault tolerance keeps running despite failures. Agility is the speed of experimenting and delivering.
items.example: Capacity that shrinks overnight automatically → elasticity.

items.name: CAF perspectives vs Well-Architected pillars
items.summary: CAF guides organizational adoption; Well-Architected guides workload design.
items.details: The Cloud Adoption Framework has six perspectives (business, people, governance, platform, security, operations) for planning a transformation. The Well-Architected Framework has six pillars (operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, sustainability) for reviewing architectures.
items.example: Training staff for the cloud → CAF people perspective. Designing for automatic recovery → Well-Architected reliability pillar.
items.tip: Security appears in both frameworks; read the context.

items.name: Rehost vs replatform vs refactor vs repurchase
items.summary: No changes; small optimizations; re-architect; replace with another product.
items.details: Rehost (lift and shift) moves as is. Replatform makes a few cloud optimizations, such as moving to a managed database. Refactor rebuilds for cloud-native features. Repurchase moves to a different product, often SaaS.

items.name: Responsibility on EC2 vs RDS vs Lambda
items.summary: More managed service → more AWS responsibility.
items.details: On EC2 the customer patches the guest OS and runtime. On RDS AWS patches the OS and database engine. On Lambda AWS runs the servers and runtime. In every case the customer owns data, access, and configuration.
